studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement about belief, start by naming out loud what you and the other person actually agree on. Say it in one sentence, before anything else. Then stop and let them respond to that. The order in this ayah is the whole method. Most conversations of this kind fail because the shared sentence is never said.
studies.explainEasier: The message to Jews and Christians is simple: let us agree on one thing. We all worship God alone. Nobody should treat any other person as if they were God.

studies.title: Arguing About Abraham
studies.meaning: The question is put as a matter of sequence. Abraham lived before either the Torah or the Gospel was revealed, so a dispute over which later community he belonged to asks something the timeline cannot support. The argument is chronological rather than doctrinal, and it ends by inviting the listeners to reason it through themselves. Classical commentators note the tone: the address is direct, but the reasoning is offered rather than imposed on anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Abraham was claimed by more than one community in and around Medina, and the claim mattered because it carried authority over whose practice was original. The classical commentaries report disputes of exactly this kind taking place in the city. The surah's answer does not adjudicate between claimants; it observes that the categories being fought over came into existence after the man they are applied to.

keyTerms.note: From the root for advancing a proof. The form used makes it reciprocal, a contest of claims, and the verb recurs several times in this section of the surah as the activity being questioned.
The passive of the verb for revelation descending. Using the passive keeps attention on the timing of the event rather than on who caused it, which is exactly what the argument turns on.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, the same word behind the term for a hobble on a camel. Reason in Arabic is the faculty that restrains, holding a person back from running loose.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ancestry claims were contested in Arabia the way property was, and with the same seriousness. Tribes traced themselves to prestigious forebears, and a successful claim brought precedence, marriage prospects and a share in sanctuary custodianship. Arguments about who a distant ancestor really belonged to were not antiquarian. They settled current standing, and everyone listening knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions Abraham in twenty-five different surahs, more often than any prophet except Moses, and names him repeatedly in this one. He is the figure the Quran most consistently uses as common ground between communities, which is part of why the argument here is conducted over him rather than anyone else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit on how far a later category can be pushed backwards. Communities formed around a revelation cannot claim someone who preceded that revelation, however genuinely they trace themselves to him. That protects the earlier figure from annexation, and it also implies something about identity generally: what a person actually was is not settled by who later claims them.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about several patriarchs, asking whether you know better than God does.
Gives the conclusion two ayat later, describing what Abraham actually was.
Describes Abraham as a community in himself, upright, and not among those who associate.

studies.applyIt: Notice the shape of this argument: not a better claim, but a question about the timeline. The next time you find yourself in a dispute about who owns a tradition, a phrase, or a founder, check the dates before you weigh the merits. It settles more arguments than people expect, and it costs nothing to look.

studies.title: Neither One Nor The Other
studies.meaning: A distinction is drawn between two kinds of dispute. There is arguing about what you have some knowledge of, which the ayah notes without endorsing, and arguing about what you have none of, which it questions. Then the answer to the previous ayah comes plainly: Abraham belonged to neither of the later communities. He is described instead by two words, one meaning turned away from every false object of worship, the other meaning surrendered to God. He is not claimed for a third party; he is described.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address begun in the previous ayah. The dispute over Abraham was live in Medina because his authority underwrote claims about whose practice was original. The classical commentaries describe the argument in general terms and read the surah's answer as removing the terms of the dispute rather than deciding it, which is why the description offered uses neither community's name.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to lean or turn aside. It describes someone who has turned from every false object of worship toward God, and it was used in Arabia before Islam of individuals who kept to that alone.
The participle from the same root as the religion named earlier in this surah. Applied to a figure who long preceded any later community, it names a disposition rather than a membership.
The indefinite form is used twice, so the ayah speaks of having some knowledge of a matter rather than of expertise in it. That makes the contrast one of warrant rather than of qualification.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pre-Islamic Arabia remembered individuals who rejected the idols without belonging to any scriptural community, and the word used here for upright attached to them in ordinary speech. The audience therefore had a live sense of what it named: someone recognisably devoted to one God and recognisably outside the established religious categories of the region.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered upright appears twelve times in the Quran, and most of those occurrences describe Abraham. It is never used as the name of a community in the way the two labels rejected in this ayah are, which is part of why it works here as an alternative to both of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about the warrant for religious speech. Disagreement is not itself the fault; disagreement without knowledge is. It then answers the original question by refusing both available labels, which suggests that the categories communities use to sort themselves may not reach back to the figures they are built on. What is offered instead is a description of orientation rather than of belonging.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same claim by naming the upright way of Abraham, who associated nothing with God.
Calls him the one who named this community, carrying the description forward in time.
Describes a straight religion as the upright way of Abraham, spoken in the Prophet's own voice.

studies.applyIt: There is a specific discipline here: notice when you are arguing past the edge of what you actually know. Pick one topic you have opinions about and locate that edge honestly. Then, in the next conversation about it, say where the edge is, out loud. It is a small thing to say and unusually hard to do.

studies.title: Nearest To Abraham
studies.meaning: The question of who has a claim on Abraham is answered by a criterion rather than a lineage. Those closest to him are the ones who followed him, then the prophet addressed here, then those who believe. Classical commentators note that descent is not mentioned at all. The ayah closes by naming God the guardian of the believers, which quietly replaces the whole framework of the dispute: what was being argued over was patronage, and the last clause assigns it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, concluding the short section that began with a question about arguing over Abraham. Claims of connection to prestigious ancestors carried real authority in the region, and communities in Medina traced themselves to him. The classical commentaries read this ayah as the resolution of the argument set up two ayat earlier, replacing an inherited claim with a criterion anyone can meet or fail to meet.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root meaning to be close and to take charge. It covers proximity and the right that comes with it, so the ayah answers a question about entitlement and about closeness at once.
The verb of walking behind someone on a road. It names a relationship established by movement rather than by birth, which is precisely the shift this ayah is making.
From the same root as the comparative that opens the ayah. Ending on this word ties the two halves together: nearness to Abraham is answered by naming who is near to the believers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the structure of Arabian society. A client attached himself to a stronger party, and that bond determined who defended him, who spoke for him, and where he stood in any gathering. Claiming a great ancestor was a way of claiming a patron who could never withdraw the arrangement. The last clause of this ayah addresses exactly the need that made such claims valuable.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative that opens this ayah and the noun that closes it come from the same root, so the argument and its resolution are built out of one word. Constructions of this kind, where a passage turns on the repetition of a root in different forms, are a recognised feature of Quranic style and are largely invisible in translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belonging is redefined as following rather than descending, which makes a historic figure accessible to anyone and inheritable by no one. That has consequences beyond the immediate dispute, since it removes the possibility of a claim on God's favour held by right of birth. The closing clause completes the move by naming the relationship believers actually have, which is not a claim but a gift.

crossReferences.why: Says the covenant with Abraham does not reach the wrongdoers among his own descendants.
Applies the same connection to the community addressed, calling it the way of Abraham.
Names God the guardian of those who believe, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are counting on that you did not earn: a family reputation, a school, a community you were born into. None of it is bad to have. But this ayah puts following where inheritance was, so pick one thing you have inherited and identify the actual practice underneath it. Then do that practice this week.

studies.title: They Only Mislead Themselves
studies.meaning: A wish is described, and then its effect is reversed. Some among the People of the Book would like to lead the believers astray; what actually happens is that they lead themselves astray instead. The final clause is the sharpest part: they do not perceive it. Classical commentators note the careful limitation to a party rather than to a whole community, a qualification the surah maintains and returns to explicitly a few ayat later.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section addressing the scriptural communities of the city directly. The surah is careful with its scope, speaking of a group among them here and describing an upright group among them a few ayat later in warm terms. The classical commentaries preserve that distinction. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah, which the sources read as describing a pattern rather than one episode.

keyTerms.note: A verb of affectionate wanting rather than of plotting. It names an inclination of the heart, which is why the ayah can describe an intention without reporting that anything was done.
A word for a portion of a larger body, from a root meaning to go around. Its use here is a deliberate limitation of scope, and the surah keeps to that limitation consistently.
From the root behind the words for a poet and for fine awareness. It names subtle noticing, so the denial says the harm is not merely unadmitted but genuinely unfelt by them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guide who misled a caravan in the desert did not walk a separate road home. He was on the same route, out of water at the same hour, and the consequences of his direction reached him first. Everyone who had travelled understood that misdirection is not something you do to other people from a safe distance. The image behind this ayah was a practical fact of the trade routes.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a party used here recurs through this surah, and not only of others. It later names two groups among the believers who almost lost heart before a battle, and a group at Uhud preoccupied with their own concerns. The surah applies the same limiting term in both directions, which stops it becoming a label for one side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes a moral mechanism: an attempt to damage someone else lands first on the one attempting it, and lands invisibly. That places the primary consequence of an intention inside the person who holds it, before anything at all reaches its target. The final clause about not perceiving is what makes it serious, since a harm you cannot feel is one you have no reason to stop.

crossReferences.why: Describes an upright group among the same community, reciting through the night and prostrating.
Uses the same reversal: they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive it.
States the principle generally: an evil scheme encircles only the people who devise it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you wanted something to go badly for someone. Not acted on it, only wanted it. Notice what that wanting did to you while you carried it, and how little it did to them. The claim in this ayah is not moral advice; it is a description of where the damage actually goes.

studies.title: Truth Dressed In Falsehood
studies.meaning: Two questions are put in the same form, and both turn on one phrase: while you know. The first asks why signs are refused by people who are themselves witnesses to them. The second names two distinct acts, mixing truth with falsehood and concealing truth, and again attaches knowledge to both. Classical commentators observe that neither question asks whether the thing happened. The form assumes it and asks for a reason, which leaves the answer with the hearer.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's direct address to the scriptural communities of the city. The classical commentaries connect the passage to disagreements in Medina about what the earlier scriptures contained, without fixing it to a single episode. The surah's address in this section is consistently to a party rather than to everyone, a limitation it states explicitly a few ayat earlier and returns to later.

keyTerms.note: The verb literally means to dress something in a garment. Mixing truth with falsehood is pictured as putting the wrong clothes on a thing, so it is still there and no longer recognisable.
From a root for holding something back within, used of suppressing knowledge, evidence or grief. It names withholding what one has rather than asserting what is false.
The verb covers seeing something firsthand and testifying to it. Its use sharpens the first question, since a witness who denies is doing something different from a stranger who disbelieves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony held a society together where almost nothing was written down. A witness in a dispute over a debt, a sale or a killing was the entire evidence, and a man known to have concealed what he saw lost his standing permanently. Everyone understood the difference between lying outright and simply not saying what you knew. The second was harder to prove and just as destructive.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of clothing truth in falsehood appears more than once in the Quran, and the verb belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of dress. Arabic uses one root for a garment and for confusion, which lets the text describe a subtle misrepresentation with a completely everyday word rather than a technical one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies concealment as a wrong in its own right, separate from denial. Something can be preserved accurately, held in full knowledge, and still be withheld at the moment it would count. Because both questions specify that those addressed know, the failure named is one of will rather than of understanding, which is where this surah has already located division among people who share a text.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two acts together: do not clothe truth with falsehood, nor conceal it knowingly.
Traces division among scriptural communities to rivalry arising after knowledge had come.
Speaks of those who conceal what was sent down of clear proofs and of guidance.

studies.applyIt: Concealing is easier than lying and feels almost innocent. Think of one thing you know that would help someone if you said it, and that you have not said because saying it would cost you. You do not have to act today. Name the cost accurately to yourself first, because that is usually where the honesty is missing.

studies.title: Believe At Dawn, Refuse By Evening
studies.meaning: A tactic is quoted rather than described. Believe in the morning and reject by evening, the speakers say, so that the believers will turn back. The reasoning behind it is social: if people known to have examined the scriptures publicly reverse themselves, others will conclude there was something in it worth reversing. Classical commentators note that the passage exposes a plan simply by reporting it, which is a method the surah uses more than once in this section.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. The classical commentaries report the tactic as concerning the change in the direction of prayer, though they preserve variation in the details. The surah attributes it to a group rather than to everyone, and the wording of the plan itself suggests a proposal made among a few people rather than a position taken publicly.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for its first part, the way a face is the front of a person. Arabic gives the day a face and an end, so the tactic is described in the vocabulary of a body turning.
The counterpart to the opening phrase, closing the figure. The pairing marks out a single day, which is what makes the reversal conspicuous rather than gradual and unremarkable.
The verb for going back the way you came. It names the intended effect on others: not a refutation of anything, but a retracing of steps that had already been taken.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Changing religion in a tribal society was public and structural. It moved a person's alliances, altered who would defend them, and was noticed at once by everyone who mattered. Nobody changed religion privately. That is exactly what makes the tactic described here plausible: a visible reversal inside a single day would have been discussed across the whole city before nightfall.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah quotes a plan directly, in the words of those making it, which the Quran does in several places with the schemes of opponents. Classical commentators observe that reporting a private proposal in public was itself a form of answer, since the tactic depended entirely on nobody knowing that it was a tactic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes that conviction is contagious in both directions, and that people take their bearings partly from what others do. That is a realistic account of how belief actually spreads, and it is not condemned here; what is exposed is the deliberate exploitation of it. The tactic also depends on the visibility of religious commitment, which the surah elsewhere treats as a strength rather than a weakness.

crossReferences.why: Describes wavering between two sides and belonging fully to neither, in similar terms.
Portrays those who profess belief without holding it, and the sickness in their hearts.
Continues the quoted speech, adding the instruction to trust only those of your own religion.

studies.applyIt: You are more influenced by other people's confidence than you think, and so is everyone around you. Pick one commitment you have quietly softened because somebody you respect seemed unimpressed by it. Reconsider it on its own terms this week, without reference to them. The tactic in this ayah only works on people who have never done that.

studies.title: Guidance Is God's Guidance
studies.meaning: The quoted advice continues and narrows: trust only those who follow your own religion. The reply comes in two parts, each introduced by an instruction to speak. The first states that guidance belongs to God, so it is not a possession any community controls. The second names bounty as lying in God's hand, given to whom He wills. Classical commentators discuss the middle clause at length, since its structure allows more than one reading of who is speaking and where the quotation ends.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address begun in the previous ayah. The concern being answered is a real one for any community with a long tradition: the possibility that what it holds might also be given elsewhere. The classical commentaries read the passage as meeting that anxiety directly rather than dismissing it, which is why the answer concerns God's freedom to give rather than anybody's unworthiness.

keyTerms.note: Carrying the definite article, so it names guidance as one single thing rather than a quality anyone might possess. Attaching it to God removes it from the inventory of what a community can hold in trust.
From a root meaning what remains over and above, an excess. It names a gift beyond anything owed, which is why it cannot be claimed as a right by any party at all.
An active participle from the verb to be wide. It describes God as having room, which in this context means that giving to one party does not reduce what remains available to another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a world of finite wells, grazing and trade routes, most goods were genuinely rival: what one tribe used, another could not. Standing worked the same way, since precedence was a fixed quantity divided among a limited number of claimants. The description of God as vast pushes directly against that intuition, and the audience would have felt the strangeness of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The name describing God as vast, which closes this ayah, occurs several times in the Quran and is usually paired with knowledge, as it is here. Classical commentators explain the pairing as guarding against the idea that abundance means indiscriminateness: the giving is unlimited in extent and exact in its placement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about exclusivity by relocating the thing being fought over. Guidance and bounty are not shares in a limited stock but gifts from an unlimited giver, so another community receiving something does not diminish what anyone else holds. That removes the logic behind religious rivalry without denying that revelation is genuinely given to particular people at particular times.

crossReferences.why: Says God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, answering a comparable reluctance.
States plainly that guiding people is not the messenger's to do, but God's alone.
Completes the thought immediately: He singles out His mercy for whomever He wills.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you feel a small drop when someone outside your circle does well at something you care about. That reaction assumes a fixed supply. The description at the end of this ayah says there is room. Test it once this week: when the feeling arrives, say the person's name and one true good thing about what they did.

studies.title: Singled Out For Mercy
studies.meaning: One short sentence completes the previous ayah's answer and then closes on a description of God. Mercy is said to be assigned specifically, to whom God wills, with a verb meaning to set something apart for a particular recipient. Classical commentators note that the passage does not say why any given person is chosen, and that the surrounding argument does not need it to. What it establishes is where the decision sits, which is enough to settle the dispute it belongs to.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, concluding the section that answers an anxiety about revelation being given to others. The two ayat work as a pair: one says bounty is in God's hand, and this one says it is placed deliberately. The classical commentaries treat the pairing as the surah's resolution of a long argument about which community holds what, and note that no criterion is offered by either side.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to set apart for a particular case, the opposite of what is general. It describes a gift addressed to someone in particular rather than distributed at large.
From the root that also gives Arabic its word for a womb. The Quran uses this term for guidance, revelation and rain alike, so what is being assigned here is deliberately left broad.
An adjective from a root connected to bone, so the sense is of something with substance and mass rather than merely large. It describes the bounty as having weight, not only extent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gifts in Arabia were public and specific. A chief distributed at a gathering and everyone saw who received what, so a gift was as much a statement about a relationship as a transfer of goods. Being singled out mattered more than the value of the object itself. The verb used here belongs to that world, where the act of assigning was the significant part.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat that close this section end on three descriptions of God in quick succession: vast, knowing, and possessor of immense bounty. Closing a passage with divine names is a structural habit of the Quran, and commentators read the particular names chosen as summarising the argument the passage has just made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is presented as specific rather than merely general, which changes its character. A universal mercy reaching everyone equally would be a property of the world; a mercy assigned deliberately is an act, and acts have an actor with intentions. The passage leaves those intentions unexplained, which leaves the recipient holding gratitude rather than an account of why they deserved it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of God singling out His mercy for whomever He wills.
Sets up this conclusion by placing all bounty in God's hand, given to whom He wills.
Tells the People of the Book that bounty is in God's hand, given out as He wills.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing in your life you did nothing to arrange: where you were born, a person who took an interest in you early, a capacity you simply have. Name it specifically rather than in general. The verb here means singled out, and the practice it suggests is identifying what was addressed to you.

studies.title: A Heap Of Gold, A Single Coin
studies.meaning: Two kinds of person are described within the same community, and the description is scrupulously even. One will return a fortune left in his keeping; another will not return a single coin unless you stand over him. The ayah then names the belief that made the second behaviour feel permissible: that no obligation is owed to outsiders. What is condemned is less the failure to repay than the doctrine invented to license it, which the ayah says is attributed to God knowingly.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. Commercial trust between communities was ordinary in Medina, since deposits, loans and goods travelled between people who did not share a religion. The classical commentaries treat the passage as describing a real pattern of conduct while insisting on the distinction the ayah draws, since it names the trustworthy before the untrustworthy.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith, for safety and for a deposit left in trust. To entrust someone is to make yourself safe with them, which is why the same root covers belief.
The same word used earlier in this surah of heaped-up wealth. Its exact quantity was disputed by the lexicographers, but its sense of an enormous and unspecified sum never was.
The participle for standing, used of remaining insistently present. It pictures a creditor who has to physically stay there until he is paid, which is what recovery looked like without courts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina had no bank and no bailiff. A traveller leaving for a season handed his savings to someone he judged reliable, and the whole system rested on reputation. A man known to return deposits attracted business; a man who did not was avoided but could rarely be compelled. Standing over a debtor until he paid was an undignified necessity everyone had either done or watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The two amounts named in this ayah are deliberately incomparable: an unmeasured heap of gold set against one named coin. Classical rhetoricians describe this as a device in which the extremes are given so the middle is understood, and the word for the larger sum appears earlier in this surah in an entirely different argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates conduct from community. Both the trustworthy and the untrustworthy are placed inside the same group, and the ayah refuses to let either stand for the whole. Its sharper claim concerns doctrine: a rule limiting honesty to one's own people is called a lie attributed to God, which makes the theological error prior to the practical one rather than a result of it.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same refusal to generalise, describing an upright group inside the same community.
States the general principle: render trusts back to the people they belong to.
Describes a deposit given without a written record, and calls for the trust to be discharged.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your standard of honesty shifts with the person in front of you: a stranger, a large company, someone from outside your circle. It probably does, a little, and the shift usually arrives with a reason attached to it. Pick one such case this week and hold yourself to the standard you would use with a friend.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: God Loves The Mindful
studies.meaning: A single word opens the ayah and overturns what came before it: on the contrary, an obligation is owed. The correction is then stated positively rather than as a rebuke. Whoever fulfils his commitment and guards himself is loved by God. Classical commentators note the shift from a particular case to a general one, and from a named group to anyone at all, so a claim about who deserves honesty is answered by a description open to everybody.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering the claim quoted in the previous ayah that no obligation is owed to outsiders. The surah's method here is characteristic: a specific assertion is met with a general principle rather than a counter-accusation. The classical commentaries note that the reply names no community at all, which is what makes it a correction of the doctrine rather than of the people who held it.

keyTerms.note: A particle used only to contradict a negative statement, so it cannot be rendered by a simple yes. Its entire function is to overturn a denial that has just been made aloud.
From the root for completeness, used of paying a debt in full. Keeping a commitment is described as paying it out entirely, with nothing quietly withheld at the edges of it.
From a root meaning to take shelter behind something. It names people who move carefully because they are aware of what they are avoiding, rather than people who have achieved a rank.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise in Arabia was enforced by nothing but reputation and kin. There was no registry, no contract law, and no authority able to compel a man across a tribal boundary. What held the system together was that a person's word was the whole of their credit, and everyone knew whose word was good. Commitment kept was the currency the economy actually ran on.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah states what God loves and does not love more often than most chapters of the Quran, and the statements are spread across its whole length rather than gathered into one place. The pattern gives the surah a running commentary on character alongside its arguments about doctrine and history.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's love is attached here to a condition anyone can meet, and the condition is a kept promise rather than a membership or a rite. That places ordinary reliability among the things that matter ultimately. The construction matters too: the ayah does not say God loves the one who did this, but names a class, so the love is described as a settled disposition rather than a reaction.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the claim this ayah overturns, that no obligation is owed to outsiders.
Opens a whole surah with the instruction to fulfil commitments, before anything else is said.
Says a commitment will be asked about, treating the promise itself as something accountable.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small promise you made recently and have quietly let slide, the kind nobody would chase you for. Do it today, badly if necessary, rather than well next month. The word in this ayah means paid in full, and small unpaid promises are the ones that decide what people can actually rely on you for.

studies.title: Sold For A Small Price
studies.meaning: The transaction is described as a sale, and all the force of it lies in the price. What is handed over is a covenant with God and a person's own sworn word; what is received is called small, and never specified. Four consequences follow, and three of them are withdrawals rather than punishments: no speech, no look, no declaring clean. Classical commentators note that the punishment itself is named last and briefly, as though the withdrawal of regard were the heavier part of it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the discussion of trusts and commitments. The classical commentaries report several occasions for this ayah involving false oaths sworn to secure property or to win a dispute, and the reports differ in their particulars. The sources therefore treat it as a general statement about oaths taken lightly, arising in a setting where a sworn word settled cases no evidence could.

keyTerms.note: The verb of purchase, used in the Quran for trading one thing away for another. Describing this as a purchase makes the person an active party who looked at the terms and accepted them.
Deliberately left unquantified. The commentators note that any price would be small against what is given up, so the adjective describes the exchange itself rather than the sum received.

An older word for a lot assigned to someone, related to the root for creating and apportioning. It names not a reward but the share a person would otherwise have had, which is why its absence reads as loss.
From a root covering growth and purification together. It carries the sense of pronouncing someone clean as well as making them so, so the denial withholds vindication as much as cleansing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath sworn before witnesses closed a case. Where there was no document and no independent testimony, a solemn oath was the final instrument, and communities accepted it because the alternative was violence. A man who swore falsely gained the disputed property outright. The system worked only because most people believed a false oath cost more than the goods.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the three withdrawals named here, that God will not speak to them and will not declare them clean, recur together in Surah 2 in a passage about concealing revelation for a price. The Quran repeats such clusters of negations, and the addition of the third element makes this the fullest form of the formula.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consequences described are relational rather than penal. Being unspoken to, unlooked at and undeclared clean are all removals of regard, and they are listed before any mention of suffering. That suggests an account of loss centred not on pain but on the ending of a relationship, which puts the weight in a different place from where fear usually assumes it lies.

crossReferences.why: Names the same withdrawals, of those who conceal what was revealed in exchange for a price.
Warns against using oaths as an instrument of deceit, and calls the price a little thing.
States the positive form immediately before: God loves the one who fulfils his commitment.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you have actually traded your word for recently. Usually it is not money. It is convenience, or avoiding an awkward conversation, or looking better than you are. Name the price out loud, in its real currency. The argument here is entirely about the exchange rate, and most people have never checked theirs.

studies.title: Twisting With The Tongue
studies.meaning: A group is described who bend their tongues while reciting, so that what they say sounds like scripture and is taken for it. The ayah repeats itself deliberately: it is not from the Book, it is not from God. Classical commentators discuss what the twisting involved, whether alteration in delivery, in wording, or in the sense conveyed, and they preserve the range. What is not disputed is the mechanism, which relies on the authority of a voice rather than on the content of any claim.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of Medina, where recitation of the earlier scriptures was a public and respected act. The classical commentaries connect the passage to disputes about what those scriptures actually contained, and read the ayah as describing a practice rather than a single occasion. The Quran limits it to a party, as it does throughout this section.

keyTerms.note: The verb for turning something out of its straight line, used of twisting a rope or turning the head aside. Applied to tongues it makes the distortion physical rather than merely intellectual.
The plural of the organ, which in Arabic also means a language. Locating the fault in the tongue rather than in a text places it in the act of delivery, where a listener cannot inspect it.
A verb of calculation and supposition, from the root for counting. It names an estimate made under limited information, which is exactly the position of anyone listening to a recitation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in that world was heard far more often than it was read. Few could check a text, copies were rare and expensive, and authority belonged to the person reciting. A trained voice carried its own credibility, and an audience listening to a language it did not fully command had no way of testing what it heard. The vulnerability this ayah describes was structural.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for twisting appears elsewhere in the Quran of people turning their heads away, and the same root gives Arabic its word for a bend in a road. The image stays consistent across those uses: something that ought to run straight is being deflected without ever being broken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a form of dishonesty that leaves every individual statement intact. Nothing is denied and nothing openly invented; a false impression is produced by the manner of delivery alone. Treating this as a lie about God rather than about a text sets a high standard for religious speech, since it makes the impression created, not merely the words used, the thing a speaker answers for.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same twisting of tongues, adding that it is a slandering of the religion.
Speaks of writing a book with one's own hands and saying it is from God, for a small price.
Names the parallel act a few ayat earlier: clothing truth in falsehood and concealing it.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between saying something false and creating a false impression using true things. The second is far more common and much easier to excuse. Pick one situation this week where you have been technically accurate and deliberately misleading, and correct the impression rather than the words.

studies.title: No One Given Scripture Would Say
studies.meaning: The claim concerns what a prophet could not do. Someone given a book, sound judgement and prophecy would never turn round and ask people to worship him. The ayah then supplies what such a person would say instead, using a rare word for those who belong wholly to the Lord, and it grounds that condition in two ordinary activities: teaching scripture and studying it. Classical commentators note that the alternative offered is a practice rather than a rank.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's engagement with the Christian community of Najran and with wider disputes about the standing of prophets and teachers. The classical commentaries report that the ayah answers a question about whether obedience of the kind owed to God might be given to a prophet. The surah's answer speaks about prophets in general rather than about any single figure, as the whole section does.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making firm and for issuing a ruling. Named separately from the Book, it points to the capacity to apply what is known, which possession of a text does not by itself supply.

A rare word built directly on the word for Lord. The classical lexicographers connect it with deep learning joined to devotion, and describe it as naming teachers whose knowledge is turned toward God.
From a root meaning to efface by repeated passing over, as a road is worn into a track. Study in Arabic is wearing something smooth by returning to it, not acquiring it once and moving on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Teachers in the ancient world held real power over their students, and religious authority in the region ran through scholars who could read what most people could only hear. A teacher's word settled matters of practice for a whole community. The temptation this ayah describes was not hypothetical, and the audience knew of households whose loyalties followed one learned man.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for those wholly devoted to the Lord occurs only three times in the Quran, once here and twice in a later surah, always of learned teachers among earlier communities. It is among the rarest terms the Quran uses for a category of religious person, and it has no plural counterpart elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places a limit on religious authority that comes from inside the office rather than from outside it. The very gifts that make someone worth following are described as making a demand for worship impossible. It also relocates the goal of teaching: those taught are to become people of the Lord themselves, so instruction aims at independence before God rather than dependence on a teacher.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same argument: nor would he tell you to take angels and prophets as lords.
Shows Jesus questioned about exactly this, and disowning it in the plainest possible terms.
Describes a community taking its scholars and monks as lords apart from God.

studies.applyIt: If you learn from someone, a teacher, a speaker, an author, notice whether their effect is to send you toward the source or to keep you coming back to them. Both patterns are common. Test it this week by acting on one thing you learned from them without checking back in with them first.

studies.title: Angels And Prophets Are Not Lords
studies.meaning: The argument continues into its second half. The same person who could not ask to be worshipped could not instruct others to take angels or prophets as lords either, so the prohibition reaches past his own case to every intermediary. Then a question closes it: would he command refusal after you have submitted. Classical commentators note that the question does the work an argument would otherwise have to do, since the absurdity is meant to be felt rather than demonstrated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the preceding ayah as one argument. Reverence for angels and for prophets was present in several religious communities of the region, in forms the surah does not itemise. The classical commentaries treat the ayah as addressing the general principle rather than any specific practice, which is consistent with the way this whole section speaks of prophets in the plural.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word used throughout the Quran for God as Lord. Its root covers ownership, nurture and authority together, so taking someone as a lord means placing your affairs under them.
A verb of adopting or acquiring something for one's own use. It implies an act by the person doing it, rather than a status the other party has claimed or asked for.
From a root meaning to cover or bury, used of a farmer covering seed with soil. Refusal in Arabic is pictured as covering something already present rather than as failing to notice it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia before Islam recognised intermediaries as a normal religious arrangement. Deities were approached through lesser figures, and some traditions regarded certain beings as associates of the high god, an arrangement the Quran addresses elsewhere. The audience therefore understood the appeal of an intermediary immediately, having recently left a system built around one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for lord appears here in the plural, which is unusual, since the Quran normally uses it of God alone in the singular. The plural form occurs only a handful of times in the whole Book, and always inside an argument about intermediaries, which makes the grammatical number itself part of the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes a route that religious history repeatedly reopens, in which honour paid to a genuinely honourable figure gradually turns into something else. What is notable is that it does not diminish angels or prophets in order to close it; their standing is left entirely intact, and only the direction of worship is fixed. That separation of honour from worship is what the section rests on.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same plural word for lords in the invitation to a common word between communities.
Describes a comparable arrangement, taking scholars and monks as lords apart from God.
Answers a similar argument, insisting Jesus was a servant on whom favour was bestowed.

studies.applyIt: Notice who you go to first when something goes wrong. Not who you believe in, but who you actually contact. There is nothing wrong with having people you trust, and this ayah diminishes nobody. It simply asks you to know the order, and the order is visible in what you reach for first.

studies.title: The Covenant Of The Prophets
studies.meaning: A covenant is reported, taken from the prophets themselves rather than from their communities. Its terms are conditional: given scripture and wisdom, if a messenger comes confirming what you hold, you will believe in him and support him. Scholars differ over whether the pledge binds the prophets personally or their communities through them, and the classical commentaries record both readings. The scene closes with an affirmation, a call to bear witness, and God naming Himself among the witnesses.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, concluding the argument that began with what a prophet could and could not say. The passage addresses a live question in Medina: whether accepting a later messenger is a departure from an earlier covenant or one of its terms. The classical commentaries read this as the surah's answer, since it places support for a confirming messenger inside the original agreement rather than in competition with it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie firmly, related to a trusted bond and to a knot. It names an agreement made secure, and is stronger than the ordinary Arabic word for a promise.
A word for a heavy load or a tie that holds something down. It names an obligation by its weight, and the Quran uses it elsewhere of burdens people ask to be relieved of.
From a root meaning to settle and come to rest. Affirming in Arabic is letting a matter settle into place, so the question asks whether the terms have been accepted as final.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Covenants in Arabia were sealed publicly, and the witnesses present were the whole of the enforcement. Two parties spoke the terms aloud, and those standing by were expected to remember and to testify if a dispute arose later. A covenant without witnesses was nearly worthless. The scene described here follows that shape exactly, down to the call for the parties to bear witness themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: God naming Himself among the witnesses to His own covenant is a striking construction, since a witness is normally a third party to an agreement. Classical commentators discuss it as an intensification, and this surah uses witnessing language repeatedly, including in the disciples' prayer to be recorded among the witnesses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage frames prophetic succession as a matter of agreement rather than of replacement. Each prophet is described as having accepted, in advance, the obligation to support a later messenger who confirms what he holds. That makes continuity a term of the original covenant, so recognising a later revelation is presented as faithfulness to the earlier one rather than a departure from it.

crossReferences.why: Recalls a covenant taken from the prophets, naming several of them individually.
Describes a covenant taken from those given the Book, to make it clear and not conceal it.
Speaks of a messenger found described in what earlier communities already held.

studies.applyIt: Think about a commitment you made in advance, before you knew what it would require: a marriage, a job, a friendship, a faith. Covenants of that shape are agreed under one set of conditions and tested under another. Name the one you are currently inside, and what it is actually asking of you now.

studies.title: Willingly Or Unwillingly
studies.meaning: Two short ayat close the argument. The first names the consequence of turning away after affirming, and the second asks a question that widens the frame completely: is some religion other than God's being sought, when everything in the heavens and the earth has already submitted to Him, willingly or otherwise. Classical commentators explain the second phrase as covering the created order's necessary submission alongside the voluntary submission of those who choose it, without collapsing one into the other.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section on the covenant of the prophets. The question posed is general rather than aimed at any named group. The classical commentaries read the pairing as this surah's characteristic movement, from a specific dispute outward to a cosmic frame, and note that the argument here is drawn from creation rather than from scripture, so it stands independently of the debate that preceded it.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of a date breaking out of its skin. It names stepping outside a boundary rather than denying that one exists, so it describes conduct after an agreement rather than before.
A pair of verbal nouns naming the two modes of compliance. Setting them together covers the whole range without saying which creatures fall where, which lets the phrase describe everything at once.
The same verb as the religion named earlier in this surah, applied here to the heavens and the earth. Using one word for creation's submission and a human being's is the passage's central move.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world visibly obeyed something. The stars turned on a schedule navigators trusted with their lives, the seasons arrived, the camel knelt when it was made to kneel. Human beings were the conspicuous exception, the one part of the arrangement that argued back. An audience living close to the physical world would have felt the contrast the question depends on.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words for willing and unwilling occurs four times in the Quran. Three of those describe the whole created order submitting or prostrating, and one describes human spending. The phrase is almost reserved for statements about creation as a whole, which is precisely how this ayah uses it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds a religious claim in a cosmological observation rather than in a text, which lets it address anyone at all. If submission is what everything else already does, then the human question is not whether to submit but whether to do it knowingly. That distinction, between compliance and consent, is where this passage locates the whole significance of human choice.

crossReferences.why: Says everything in the heavens and earth prostrates to God, willingly or unwillingly.
Reports the heavens and the earth answering that they come willingly when summoned.
Supplies the covenant that turning away, in the first of these two ayat, refers back to.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your day you already spend complying with things you never chose: gravity, tiredness, the need to eat, other people's schedules. The question here is not whether you will submit to anything. It is which of your compliances you have ever actually agreed to. Pick one and agree to it deliberately today.

studies.title: We Make No Distinction
studies.meaning: A statement of belief is given in the form of a list, and the list is deliberately long: what was revealed here, what was given to Abraham and his line, what Moses and Jesus and the prophets received. Then the clause that carries the weight: no distinction is made between any of them. Classical commentators read this as refusing selective acceptance, the practice of receiving one messenger and declining another, rather than as a claim that all prophets are identical in rank.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the covenant of the prophets and its consequences. The declaration is placed in the community's own mouth as an answer to a dispute about which revelations count. The classical commentaries note that a nearly identical statement appears in an earlier surah, and read the repetition here as its application to the specific arguments this chapter has been conducting.

keyTerms.note: A word for the lines descending from Jacob's sons, from a root associated with extension. It names a lineage collectively rather than any individual, which keeps the list from becoming a roll of names.
An intensive verb for dividing a thing into parts. Denying it means refusing to sort the messengers into accepted and rejected, which is exactly the practice the ayah is answering.
The participle from the root this surah uses for the religion God accepts. Placing it at the very end turns the whole preceding list into an account of what that submission consists of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances in Arabia were held or broken one clan at a time, and a party could be at peace with one branch of a tribe while at war with another. Selective recognition was the ordinary shape of politics. The refusal to distinguish, stated here about messengers, ran against a habit of mind the audience applied to nearly every relationship they had.
studies.didYouKnow: A nearly identical declaration appears twice in Surah 2, with small differences in wording and in who is speaking. Comparing the three versions is a standard exercise in the commentaries, since the variations show one creed placed in different mouths and put to work in different arguments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defines faith partly by what it refuses to do. Accepting some messengers and rejecting others is treated as a single error whichever ones are chosen, because it makes the believer the one doing the selecting. The list is also strikingly inclusive of figures other communities claim, which turns a creed into a statement of overlap rather than of difference.

crossReferences.why: Gives almost the same declaration, with the same list and the same refusal to distinguish.
Describes those who believe in some messengers and disbelieve in others, and names it plainly.
Places the same words in the mouths of the believers, adding that they hear and obey.

studies.applyIt: Read the list slowly and notice how many of these names belong to communities you may think of as other. The creed you hold already contains them. If you have ever spoken about those communities as though they had nothing to do with you, read this ayah twice before the next such conversation.

studies.title: What Will Not Be Accepted
studies.meaning: The word translated Islam is the verbal noun for surrender to God, and the ayah says that anything sought as a religion other than that will not be accepted. Read alongside the surah's earlier definition and the list of prophets just given, classical commentators understand the term as naming the disposition every prophet taught rather than a community set apart from them. The verb for seeking matters too: it describes a person going after something, not one who has never encountered it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately following the declaration of belief in every messenger. The order is significant and the classical commentaries note it: the creed naming Abraham, Moses and Jesus comes first, and this ayah follows on from it, so the two are read together. The surah has already defined the term in question earlier, in a passage about division arising after knowledge came.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb to seek, describing deliberate pursuit. It names someone actively going after an alternative rather than someone who has simply not been reached by anything.
The verbal noun from the root for handing something over whole. This surah has already used it for what every prophet brought, and that is the sense the commentators carry into this ayah.
From the vocabulary of trade, naming a merchant whose venture returns less than it cost him. It describes the outcome of a transaction rather than a penalty imposed from outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade was the frame through which Arabians understood risk. A merchant put capital into a caravan and either returned with profit or came back short, and the word for that shortfall was ordinary commercial vocabulary. Describing a life's outcome as a loss was not an insult but an accounting term, and it landed on people who had watched ventures fail.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for religion and the word used for surrender both appear earlier in this surah, in a single ayah that sets out their relationship. The two passages sit more than sixty ayat apart, and the second assumes the definition given in the first, which is one of the ways this surah builds an argument across its length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah's force depends on what its central term means, and the surah has taken care to define that term before using it here. Understood as surrender to God, the claim is not that a label is required but that a posture is, and the list of prophets just given is what shows the posture running through every revelation. That keeps the statement demanding without making it a question of membership.

crossReferences.why: Defines the same term earlier in this surah, as the religion accepted with God.
Supplies the creed immediately before, naming every prophet without distinction.
Describes whoever surrenders his face to God while doing good as having his reward.

studies.applyIt: The word at the centre of this ayah means handing something over whole. Pick one area of your life you have kept back, not out of defiance but because you never got round to it. Name it specifically. Then hand over the smallest decision inside it today, and notice what that actually feels like.

studies.title: After They Had Believed
studies.meaning: A question is asked rather than a verdict handed down, and the question is about guidance rather than punishment: how would God guide people who refused after belief, after testifying that the messenger is true, and after clear proofs reached them. Classical commentators note that the ayah stacks three stages of knowledge before the refusal, so what is described is not a mistake but a reversal. The closing clause generalises it and names the condition wrongdoing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentaries report occasions involving individuals who left the community and later sought to return, and the reports vary in their details and in whom they concern. Because they differ, the sources read the ayah as a general statement about reversal after knowledge, and they give particular weight to the ayah a few lines later that opens a door back.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative of manner rather than of possibility. It asks by what route guidance could reach such a person, which leaves the answer open in a way that a flat denial would not.
From a root meaning to be distinct and separated out. The word names evidence that has already done its work of distinguishing, so it describes clarity achieved rather than merely offered.
From a root meaning darkness and, in usage, putting a thing where it does not belong. Wrongdoing in Arabic is misplacement, which is why one word covers injustice and associating others with God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reversal in a tribal society was socially catastrophic and therefore rare. Leaving a community meant leaving its protection, and returning meant facing everyone who had watched you go. People did it anyway, under pressure from family, from debt or from fear. The audience knew individual cases, which is part of why the surah addresses the situation directly rather than abstractly.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage runs to four ayat and its severity is reversed in the last of them, which opens with a single word meaning except. The structure is characteristic of the Quran, where extended warnings are frequently closed by an exception clause naming those who turn back and put matters right.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the difficulty in the person rather than in God's willingness. Guidance is not described as withheld out of anger but as having nothing left to work with, since everything guidance normally supplies has already been supplied and set aside. Calling the condition wrongdoing rather than error also frames it as a matter of what was done with knowledge, not of what was understood.

crossReferences.why: Reverses this passage three ayat later, excepting those who repent and set things right.
Describes repeated movement in and out of belief, and its effect on the possibility of guidance.
Distinguishes one compelled to speak against faith from one who opens his chest to refusal.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this is a question and not a sentence, and notice where the passage goes three ayat later, which is to an exception. If you are carrying something you believe has put you outside the door, read to the end of the passage before deciding. Most people stop at the severity and never reach the clause that follows.

studies.title: Except Those Who Turn Back
studies.meaning: Three ayat move from the heaviest language in the section to its reversal. The first names a penalty as the rejection of God, the angels and all people; the second says it is not lightened and no reprieve is granted; the third begins with a single word meaning except, and everything before it is qualified. Classical commentators note that repentance alone is not what is named. It is paired with putting things right, so an inward turn is joined to a repair that can be seen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about reversal after belief. The classical commentaries report that individuals in this situation did return, and that the exception clause was understood as applying to real cases rather than standing as a formality. The sources treat the sequence as deliberate: the severity is stated fully first, so that the exception cannot be read as a softening of what was said.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to drive away and expel. The English word curse suggests an incantation; the Arabic describes a distancing, being put outside rather than being harmed by a formula.
A passive verb from the root for lightness of weight. It pictures the punishment as a load, so relief would mean a reduction in what is carried rather than a shortening of the time it lasts.
The verb for returning to a place you came from. Repentance in Arabic is a change of direction rather than an emotion, which is why the ayah can pair it with a visible action.
From the root for soundness and for reconciliation between people. It names mending what was damaged, and its inclusion here keeps the turning from being a purely inward event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being driven out was the harshest thing an Arabian community could do to a person. Expulsion removed protection entirely and left a man free to be killed without consequence, which is why exile was reserved for the gravest offences. Readmission was possible but required a public act of repair, usually compensation. The vocabulary of these ayat maps closely onto that procedure.
studies.didYouKnow: The exception clause here is the third element of a three-ayah unit, and the word it opens with is the shortest in the passage. Classical commentators point out that the Quran frequently attaches such clauses to its severest statements, and that their placement, always after the warning has been completed, is consistent across those cases.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure carries the theology. By stating the full weight of a consequence and then admitting an exception, the passage keeps both seriousness and possibility intact, where either on its own would distort the picture. Pairing the turn with repair says something further: the door back is open, and it opens onto work rather than onto a declaration.

crossReferences.why: Poses the question this passage answers, about guidance after knowledge was set aside.
States the widest form of the same promise, telling servants not to despair of God's mercy.
Joins repentance to righteous action, and describes evil deeds being exchanged for good.

studies.applyIt: If there is something you have decided is past mending, notice that this passage names two things rather than one: turning back, and repairing. The second is usually the part that has actually been avoided. Pick the smallest piece of repair available to you, something concrete and doable this week, and do that first.

studies.title: Deeper Than A Single Turn
studies.meaning: The previous ayat opened a door for those who turn back and repair. This one describes a case where the door is described as closed, and the wording is precise: refusal after belief, and then an increase in refusal. Classical commentators note that the second clause carries the weight, since what is described is not one reversal but a settled and deepening direction. Several read the closing of repentance as belonging to the moment of death, when turning has become impossible rather than merely unwanted.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the exception clause that admitted those who repent. The two ayat are read together in the commentaries, since one opens what the other appears to close. The classical sources connect the passage to individuals who left the community and kept moving away from it. Reports differ over the particulars, so the commentaries treat the description as a general one.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form of the verb to add, so the increase is something done to oneself. It describes accumulation over time rather than a single act, which is what separates this case from the previous ayah.
The noun from the verb for returning. Naming it as a possession, their turning, points at something offered rather than at an inward state, which is why commentators discuss when it is offered.
From a root used of a traveller losing the road and of a thing mislaid. It names being off the path rather than opposing it, which is a different image from defiance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller who took a wrong turn in the desert could correct it within an hour and be fine. The same wrong turn, continued for a day, carried him past the wells he knew and beyond the reach of his own memory of the route. Distance did the damage, not the original error. Every caravan traveller understood that a mistake grew costlier the longer you kept going.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it sit side by side and pull in opposite directions, one admitting repentance and one describing it as unaccepted. Classical commentators treat the pairing as deliberate rather than contradictory, and a good deal of discussion in the commentary literature concerns exactly how the two are to be held together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes a reversal from a direction. What is described as beyond acceptance is not one act but a course continued and added to, which places the difficulty in accumulated momentum rather than in the severity of any single decision. Read beside the ayah before it, the two together describe an open door and the possibility of walking too far from it to turn.

crossReferences.why: Opens the door this ayah appears to close, for those who turn back and put things right.
Says repentance is not for those who persist until death arrives at the door.
Describes faith arriving too late to benefit, once the consequence is already visible.

studies.applyIt: The difference this ayah draws is between a mistake and a direction. Look at something you have been doing that you already know is wrong, and ask honestly whether you are still at the first stage or have been adding to it for a while. Then turn now rather than later, because the distinction here is about distance.

studies.title: The Earth Full Of Gold
studies.meaning: The largest sum the language can construct is named and then refused. An amount of gold equal to the whole earth would not be accepted as a ransom from someone who died refusing. Classical commentators observe that the ayah does not call the gold worthless; it says the payment will not be taken, which is a statement about the transaction rather than about the metal. The closing clause repeats a formula used earlier in the surah about having nobody to help.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the sequence about reversal after belief. The passage speaks of a condition at the moment of death rather than of any living person, which the classical commentaries emphasise, since the argument turns on the finality of the state and not on its severity. No particular occasion is reported, and the sources read it as a general statement following the discussion before it.

keyTerms.note: A construction naming the amount needed to fill something. Applied to the earth it produces the largest quantity ordinary Arabic can express, without naming any number at all.
From the root for redeeming a captive by payment, a familiar transaction across Arabia. It assumes a world in which almost anything could be settled for the right price.
Specified rather than left as wealth in general. Gold was the one commodity whose value held across borders and across generations, which is why it stands here for value itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was ordinary. Captives taken in raids were returned for payment, blood claims were settled in camels, and even a life could be priced. The system was practical rather than cynical, since it kept feuds from consuming whole tribes. In that world, being told a payment would not be accepted was stranger than being told the price was high, because it meant leaving the system altogether.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of the earth's fill of gold offered as ransom appears elsewhere in the Quran with a variation, where those who wronged would offer everything on earth and as much again alongside it. The figure recurs in several places and always describes an exchange that cannot be made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage marks the boundary of exchange. Almost everything in the audience's world could be settled by payment, and the ayah names the largest payment imaginable in order to say that this particular matter is not of that kind. What is described is a difference of category rather than a shortfall in the amount, which is why the closing clause about helpers follows so naturally.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image, everything on earth offered again over, and refused as ransom.
Denies that any ransom will be taken or intercession accepted on that day.
Ends with the identical phrase about having no helpers, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice how many of your problems you quietly solve with money or with something equivalent: time bought, tasks paid away, discomfort outsourced. That is not wrong and it works. Then name one thing in your life that is genuinely not of that kind. Most people can find one, and most people avoid looking at it.

studies.title: Until You Give What You Love
studies.meaning: Two distinct movements sit in this unit. The first places a condition on goodness itself: you will not reach it until you spend from what you love, so the measure named is attachment rather than amount. The second turns to an argument about food, saying that everything was permitted to the Children of Israel except what Israel restricted for himself before the Torah came down, and then invites the disputing party to bring the Torah and read it aloud.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentators report that companions of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) responded to the first ayah at once by giving away particular possessions they valued most, and the reports of who gave what vary while agreeing on the pattern. The second ayah belongs to the surah's discussion with the scriptural communities of Medina about which dietary restrictions were original, and it issues a challenge to produce the text.

keyTerms.note: A word for wide-reaching good, from a root associated with open land. It covers devotion, kindness to parents and honest dealing at once, which is why the Quran uses it as a summary term.
The verb for laying out money, from a root also connected with a tunnel and with something running out. Spending in Arabic is described by depletion rather than by transfer to someone else.
The ordinary verb for love, used here of possessions. Its presence shifts the condition from a quantity to a relationship, since two people giving the same sum are not doing the same thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was specific and named. A man did not own a portfolio; he owned a particular date grove, a particular well, a named horse. Everyone knew which property was whose, and which of a man's holdings he cared about most. Giving from what you loved was therefore a public and identifiable act, and the community could see exactly what had changed hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for goodness is the same one that anchors a well-known passage in Surah 2, where goodness is defined not as facing a direction in prayer but as a list of beliefs and practical acts. The two passages define one term from different angles, one by content and one by cost.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The condition set here makes generosity a matter of the giver's interior rather than of the recipient's benefit. A gift that costs nothing may still help someone, but it is described as not reaching the thing named. That places attachment at the centre of the moral question, and the closing clause, that God knows whatever is spent, extends the point to gifts nobody ever sees.

crossReferences.why: Defines the same word for goodness by a list of beliefs and acts rather than by direction.
Warns against giving away the poor part of what you have, which you would not take yourself.
Describes feeding others while loving the food, and wanting nothing back for it.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and find something you would rather not give away. That is this ayah's measure, and it has nothing to do with the price. You do not have to part with that object. But give something this week whose absence you would actually notice, and see whether it registers differently.

studies.title: The First House For People
studies.meaning: Three ayat move from a warning to an instruction to a claim about a place. Anyone inventing about God after the challenge just issued is named a wrongdoer; then the instruction is to follow the way of Abraham, described again as inclining to God and not among those who associate; then the argument shifts ground entirely, to the first house established for humanity. Classical commentators read the third ayah as answering a question of precedence by pointing to a building older than the dispute.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the classical commentaries connect the passage to arguments in Medina about which sanctuary held priority. The community had recently been directed to face Mecca in prayer, so the question was live. The surah's answer is chronological rather than polemical, in keeping with the argument it made earlier about the timing of the Torah and the Gospel relative to Abraham himself.

keyTerms.note: A word for the whole practice a community follows, distinct from the word for religion used elsewhere in this surah. It names a road walked by a group rather than an allegiance owed to someone.

A name for the valley of the sanctuary, used only here in the Quran. Classical commentators discuss its relation to the more familiar name and connect it with crowding and with people pressing together.
The passive of the verb to place. Using the passive leaves the builder unnamed at this point, which puts the weight on the house's priority in time rather than on who raised it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sanctuaries organised Arabian life. Trade fairs, truces and pilgrimage seasons clustered around them, and the tribe holding custodianship of one drew income and standing from it. Priority claims between sanctuaries were therefore economic as much as religious. The audience heard a claim about which house came first as a claim about where the centre of the peninsula actually lay.
studies.didYouKnow: The name used for the sanctuary's valley in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran, while the more familiar name appears exactly once, in a later surah. Classical lexicographers connect the form used here with a root meaning to crowd or press together, which they relate to the density of people around the house.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds a claim in chronology rather than in merit, the same move the surah made about Abraham and the later scriptures. What is asserted is priority in time and universality in purpose: a house set down for people, not for a tribe, and described as guidance for all beings. That framing makes the place a sign rather than a possession, which is how the next ayah treats it.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham and his son raising the foundations of the same house, and praying over it.
Uses the same chronological argument earlier in this surah, about Abraham and the scriptures.
Describes the site of the house being appointed to Abraham, with instructions for its use.
