studies.applyIt: The argument here rests on what came first. Try applying that to something you inherited without asking: a family habit, a way of marking a season, a phrase you use often. Find out where it actually started. Knowing the origin of a practice usually changes how tightly you hold the version you were handed.

studies.title: Whoever Enters It Is Secure
studies.meaning: The house is described by what is in it and what happens there. There are clear signs, and one is named: the place where Abraham stood. Then a statement of security, which classical commentators read both as the historical safety of the sanctuary and as the safety of one who comes to it seeking God. The pilgrimage is described as owed to God by those able to make the journey, with capability named in the same breath. The closing clause is unexpectedly gentle in its logic: God has no need of anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the section arguing about the precedence of the sanctuary. The classical commentaries place the ayah in the period before the community had access to Mecca, which was still closed to them, so the passage describes a journey its first hearers could not yet make. That timing is part of how the sources read it: the description came well before the opportunity did.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb to stand. It names the spot where someone stood rather than a monument, so the sign is a location marked by an act rather than by anything built on it.
From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith and for trust. Safety and belief share a root, so entering the house in security and entering it in faith are covered by one word family.
From a root meaning to be rich and to do without. It states that God gains nothing from any of this, which places the whole practice on the side of the one performing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary's inviolability was the one reliable truce in Arabia. Men who would kill each other on the open road stood beside one another inside its bounds, and traders travelled to its seasons under a safety no tribe would breach. Blood feuds paused there. That security was the peninsula's most valuable institution, recognised even by those who kept idols inside the house.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the standing place of Abraham occurs twice in the Quran, once in this ayah and once in an earlier surah where the instruction is to take it as a place of prayer. Both occurrences attach it to the same sanctuary, and no description of its appearance is given anywhere in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause is the theologically striking part. After describing a journey people undertake at real cost, the passage says God has no need of any of it. That takes the transaction out of the picture entirely: nothing is being supplied to God, so whatever the journey accomplishes happens inside the one who makes it. The security promised at the house works the same way, received rather than earned.

crossReferences.why: Names the same standing place and instructs that it be taken as a place of prayer.
Describes the call going out, and people arriving from every deep mountain pass.
States the same point generally: you are the needy ones, and God is free of need.

studies.applyIt: Notice the phrase about God having no need of any of it. Whatever you do today that you think of as religious, nothing is being delivered to anyone. It changes the flavour of an act to remember that its whole effect lands on you. Hold one small practice today with that in mind and see what shifts.

studies.title: Why Turn Others Away
studies.meaning: Two questions are put in parallel, each opening with an instruction to speak. The first asks why the signs are refused when God witnesses what is done. The second asks something heavier: why turn away from God's path those who have believed, seeking to put a bend in it. Classical commentators note the shift from a person's own refusal to their effect on others, and that both questions close by naming God as watching rather than by naming a consequence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. The classical commentaries connect this section to efforts to unsettle members of the young community, by reopening old tribal grievances and by raising doubts about the new direction of prayer. Reports of the specific incidents vary, so the sources read the ayat as describing a pattern of activity rather than a single episode.

keyTerms.note: The verb for barring someone from a road, used of physical obstruction as well as of dissuading. It names an effect on another person's movement rather than on their opinion.
A noun for a bend or a warp, used of a stick that will not lie straight. Applied to a path it means introducing a deviation, so the road still leads somewhere but no longer where it did.
The plural of one who testifies and one who is present. The word is used of the people addressed and, in the singular, of God two lines earlier, which sets two kinds of witnessing against each other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A road in Arabia could be spoiled without being closed. Moving a cairn, filling a well, or giving a traveller a slightly wrong bearing sent a caravan into country it could not cross. Nobody had to block anything. Deviation was the cheap and deniable form of obstruction, and everyone who travelled knew how small an alteration it took.
studies.didYouKnow: Both ayat close on God's awareness rather than on a threat, and they use two different formulations: that God witnesses what is done, and that God is not unaware of it. The second is a double negative, a construction Arabic uses to assert something more emphatically than the plain positive would.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates refusing something yourself from preventing someone else reaching it, and treats the second as the graver matter by giving it the longer question. That implies a responsibility extending past one's own commitments to the effect one has on other people's. Ending both questions on observation rather than punishment leaves the weight where this surah usually places it, in being seen.

crossReferences.why: Names those who disbelieve and turn others from the path of God, joining the two acts.
Describes those who bar others from God's way and seek to make it crooked, in similar words.
Uses the same pair of verbs of those who bar from the path and want a bend in it.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between not doing something yourself and making it harder for somebody else. Think of a person in your life who is trying to become more serious about something good, and notice whether your reaction has made that easier or slightly more awkward for them. Adjust one small thing about how you respond next time.

studies.title: Who You Listen To
studies.meaning: The address turns, and it is now the believers being spoken to. The warning is not about argument but about compliance: if you go along with a party of those given the Book, they will send you back after your belief. Classical commentators note the verb, which means returning a thing the way it came, and the limitation to a party rather than a whole community, which this surah maintains throughout. What is described is influence rather than compulsion.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the classical commentaries connect this ayah and the ones following to an incident in which old hostilities between the two main tribes of Medina were deliberately revived, nearly leading to fighting between people recently reconciled. The reports agree on the shape of the episode while differing on details. The passage about holding to God's rope, three ayat later, is read as its answer.

keyTerms.note: The verb for willing compliance, from a root meaning to do something readily. It describes going along with someone rather than being persuaded by them, which is why the warning chooses it.
From the root meaning to return a thing to where it came from. It pictures a reversal as a journey retraced rather than as a new position somebody has arrived at.
One of the limiting words this surah uses repeatedly. Its presence keeps the warning attached to particular people acting in a particular way, rather than to a whole community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two great tribes of Medina had fought a long and exhausting war before the community formed, ending only a few years earlier. The grievances were fresh, the dead were remembered by name, and men who now prayed together had faced one another in the field. Reviving that memory required no invention at all. It only required someone to raise it at the right moment.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah opens a short passage containing one of the most quoted lines in the surah, the instruction to hold fast to God's rope together and not to separate. The warning and the remedy stand three ayat apart, and classical commentators read them as a single unit responding to one incident.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies compliance rather than argument as the point of danger. A person can hear a case out and remain unmoved, but going along with someone changes what they become. That makes the choice of whom to follow consequential in itself, before any particular claim is examined. The remedy the surah supplies a few lines later is correspondingly social rather than intellectual.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer three ayat later: hold to God's rope together, and do not separate.
Shows people on that day saying they obeyed their chiefs, and were led off the path.
Describes regret over a companion who turned someone away after the reminder had come.

studies.applyIt: Think about whose approval you actually adjust yourself for. Not who you admire, but who you would soften a position in front of. Everyone has someone. Name one, and recall what you last altered because of them. This passage is not asking you to cut anyone off, only to watch the mechanism working.

studies.title: Hold On Until The End
studies.meaning: The passage asks how anyone could reject, when the revelation is being recited among them and the Messenger is present. The question is really a reproach. The answer comes in the same breath, as a remedy. Whoever takes firm hold of God has been guided to a straight path. The next line raises the standard, asking for reverence as it is due. Then it attaches that to the moment of death. So the instruction is about lasting, not about starting.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. The classical sources tie this passage to a specific incident. Someone tried to reopen the old feud between the two main Arab clans of Medina by reciting poetry about a battle they had fought before the migration. The reports describe men reaching for weapons before the quarrel was calmed. These ayat and the ones right after them came down in that setting, which is why they turn at once to unity.

keyTerms.note: The verb for gripping something to save yourself, used of clinging to a rock or a rope. It implies a body in danger rather than a mind in agreement, and it returns two ayat later as a command.

Literally the due of being mindful of Him. The construction sets no measurable limit, and early scholars note that a later ayah, telling believers to be mindful as far as they are able, is read alongside it.

The instruction is not to die but to be in this condition whenever death comes. Arabic can express that with a single participle, which is why the line reads as a command about continuity rather than about dying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two clans being addressed had fought a war within living memory. Many men in the mosque had lost fathers or brothers on the other side. Feuds in that culture were kept alive by recitation. A poem naming a killing held an obligation open for generations. One well-chosen verse recited in a marketplace could restart a conflict that had cost hundreds of lives. That is exactly what these ayat interrupted.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for taking firm hold turns up again as a direct command two ayat later. There the community is told to hold to the rope of God together and not to divide. Early scholars read the pair as one movement. The individual grip is described first, then the same grip is made collective, with the incident behind them supplying the reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reverence is set at an unlimited standard. It is then tied to endurance rather than intensity. That shifts the whole demand from peaks to continuity. Placing the instruction at the moment of death, which nobody can schedule, means it can only be met by being in that state always. And the remedy offered for wavering is not more effort. It is attachment: holding on to something outside yourself.

crossReferences.why: Turns the individual grip into a collective one and names the feud that these ayat healed.
Instructs mindfulness of God as far as you are able, read alongside the standard set here.
Shows Jacob giving his sons the same charge, not to die except in surrender to God.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are currently holding on to when things get difficult: a person, a plan, a distraction. Name it honestly, without deciding it is wrong. Then choose one moment in the coming week, when the difficulty arrives, to reach for prayer first instead. The word used here is about grip, and grip is trained by repetition rather than resolved by decision.
studies.explainEasier: God asks how people can turn away when His words are being read to them. Hold on to God and you stay on the right road. Stay that way right up to the end of your life.

studies.title: The Rope And The Pit
studies.meaning: One command with two halves: hold on together, and do not fracture. The word for holding is the same one used for gripping a rock above a drop. Then the reasoning arrives as memory rather than argument. You were enemies, He joined your hearts, and by that favour you became brothers. The final image is a ledge above a fire pit and a hand pulling you back, which makes the previous hostility a survived catastrophe rather than an unfortunate past.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this is one of the more securely reported occasions in it. The classical sources describe an attempt to revive the memory of a battle fought between Medina's two main Arab clans before the migration. They describe the anger it raised in men who had been reconciled only a few years earlier. These ayat came down to that gathering. The word for brothers in the ayah described a relationship those men had recently been fighting against.

keyTerms.note: A rope let down to someone below, used in Arabic for a pact of protection between tribes. Early scholars gloss it as the Quran, as the covenant, or as both, and record the range without deciding.
A reflexive form: the splitting is something the group does to itself. Arabic marks that grammatically, so the warning is against self-inflicted fracture rather than against being divided by others.
The verb for making things familiar and joining them into a whole, related to the word for composing a book. It describes intimacy created rather than a truce imposed, which is the ayah's claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina before the migration had been a town at war with itself. The two main Arab clans had fought for years, with the last major battle within living memory of most adults in the mosque. Alliances with the town's other communities had shifted through it. Men praying in the same row had killed each other's relatives. The word brothers in this ayah was not sentimental language; it named a recent and improbable fact.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of a rope reaching down was familiar in a specific legal sense. An agreement of protection extended by a strong tribe to a weaker one was described in exactly that language. Early scholars note that the picture therefore carries an obligation on both sides. The party holding the rope is bound by the pact as well as saved by it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unity is credited to God, not to human bargaining. That makes division a form of ingratitude as well as a political failure. The passage also recasts a community making peace as a rescue. That raises the stakes a long way. And the rope is single. So the togetherness is not a deal between the parties but a result of what each one is holding.

crossReferences.why: States that no wealth could have joined these hearts, and that God did it.
Names believers as brothers and instructs reconciliation between them as the response.
Gives the individual version of the same grip, in the ayat immediately before this one.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship in your community that was repaired and has quietly started fraying again. A family branch, a group of friends, people at your mosque. Do the small, unglamorous thing this week, the message or the visit, before the fraying becomes a position. The ayah treats division as a fire. You have already been pulled back from it once.
studies.explainEasier: Hold on to God together and do not split apart. Remember that you used to be enemies. God brought your hearts together and made you brothers. You were at the edge of a fire and He pulled you back.

studies.title: A Group That Calls To Good
studies.meaning: A group is to exist within the community with three tasks: calling to what is good, urging what is recognised as right, and holding people back from what is wrong. The order matters, since the invitation comes before either instruction. Those who do this are named as the ones who succeed. The second line gives the warning by contrast. It points to communities that split and argued after clear evidence had reached them. So the danger is put in division, not in ignorance.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines come straight after the ayat that healed a near-fatal quarrel between Medina's two main Arab clans. Early scholars read the placement as the constructive half of that episode. Having stopped the community from breaking apart, the passage gives it a task. The reference to those who divided after clear proofs reached them is generally read as pointing to earlier communities, not to any group in the town.

keyTerms.note: A group with a shared purpose rather than a shared ancestry. The Quran uses it of nations, of religious communities, and once of a single man, so its size is set by its function.
From the root for knowing. It names good that a society already acknowledges, which grounds the work in shared understanding rather than in a standard the audience has never heard.
The exact opposite construction, from the root for denying or failing to recognise. The pair frames moral work as reminding people of what they know rather than as introducing something foreign.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina had no police force and no standing court. Order was kept by clan elders and by public reputation. It was also kept by ordinary men willing to speak up in a market or a courtyard when something was wrong. A community that would not correct itself had nothing else to fall back on. Giving this work to a group within the town described something the audience already knew. It was the difference between a working settlement and a lawless one.
studies.didYouKnow: The paired terms for recognised good and rejected wrong occur together in nine ayat of the Quran. The pairing became the standard name for a whole field of Islamic writing on right conduct. Early scholars debated the grammar of this ayah. Some read the group described as a special part of the community. Others read it as the community as a whole. Both readings survive.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moral duty is shown as shared and organised, not left to each person's conscience. That makes the health of a community a religious matter. Putting the invitation first sets the tone. The work begins by calling people toward something. It does not begin by stopping them. And the failure named is division after clear evidence. So unity is treated as a condition for the work, not a reward for it.

crossReferences.why: Attributes the same three tasks to the community as a whole and calls it brought forth for humanity.
Sets out how the calling is to be done: with wisdom, good instruction, and the better argument.
Names urging one another to truth and to patience as what saves people from loss.

studies.applyIt: The next time you see something wrong in a group you belong to, start with the first of the three tasks rather than the third. Say what the better thing would look like before you say what is wrong with the current one. It is slower and it works more often. This ayah puts the invitation first for a reason.
studies.explainEasier: Some people in every community should call others to do good. They should speak up against wrong. Do not be like the groups who broke apart and argued after the truth was made clear to them.

studies.title: Faces On That Day
studies.meaning: A day is described entirely through faces. Some are made bright and some are darkened, and nothing is said about what produced either. Then those in the second group are addressed with a question that is really a recollection: did you refuse after your belief. Classical commentators note that the imagery draws on ordinary Arabic usage, where a bright face means relief and vindication and a darkened one means grief and disgrace, so what is described is a condition becoming visible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the instruction to hold together and the warning about division. The classical commentaries read the imagery as the outcome of the argument preceding it, since the question put to the darkened faces repeats the exact language used earlier in the surah about refusal after belief. No occasion is reported, and the passage functions as the conclusion of a longer sequence.

keyTerms.note: A verb of colour change used in Arabic idiom for a face lit by relief or joy. It describes brightness rather than pigment, and the same root is used elsewhere of eyes dimmed by weeping.
The counterpart verb. In Arabic usage a face darkening names grief, shame or dread, and the Quran uses the same idiom elsewhere of a man receiving news he does not want.
The verb for tasting, used of experiencing something directly and personally. It makes the consequence something known from the inside rather than observed, which is why the Quran uses it here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces did the work of documents in Arabia. Judgements were delivered in gatherings, and a man's outcome was read off him as he walked back to his people before he had said anything. Everyone present knew what a returning face meant. In a society without written verdicts, the face was where a decision became public, which is why the image needed no explaining.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this same pair of colour verbs for faces in a later surah, describing those who lied about God, and it uses the darkening idiom elsewhere of a man told he has a daughter. The imagery belongs to ordinary Arabic speech before it belongs to any scene of judgement at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes an outcome without describing a verdict, so what appears on that day is presented as a condition becoming visible rather than a sentence being announced. That suggests the state exists beforehand and is merely disclosed, which is a different picture from a trial whose result is in doubt. The question put to the darkened faces reinforces it: they are asked to recognise, not informed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half immediately: those with bright faces are inside God's mercy, remaining.
Describes faces on that day radiant and looking, and others drawn and expecting disaster.
Pairs bright laughing faces with faces covered over by dust and darkness.

studies.applyIt: Faces give people away long before words do. Spend a day noticing your own: in a mirror after a difficult conversation, or reflected in a dark screen. Not to judge it, only to see what it is already telling anyone who looks. This passage assumes a life becomes visible eventually, and some of that visibility begins early.

studies.title: God Desires No Injustice
studies.meaning: The other half of the scene arrives in a single clause, and the phrasing is spatial: those with bright faces are inside God's mercy, remaining there. Mercy is described as a place rather than a feeling. The passage then steps back twice, saying that these are God's signs recited in truth and that God desires no injustice for anyone, and finally that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him and all matters return to Him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long section that ran from the warning about division through to the imagery of faces. The classical commentaries treat these three ayat as a summary of everything argued since the surah's discussion with the scriptural communities began, since they state the principle underlying all of it and then place the whole matter into God's hands.

keyTerms.note: A preposition of containment. Mercy is described as something entered and remained within, which turns an attribute into a location, and the Quran uses the same construction of gardens.
The phrase covers truth, reality and due right together. Reciting with it means both that the content is accurate and that the reciting is properly done, and the commentators keep both senses.
A passive verb with a plural noun covering affairs, commands and situations. Nothing is said about who does the returning, which leaves the process impersonal and only the destination named.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabian life eventually went somewhere for settlement. Disputes went to an arbitrator, debts to a reckoning, a caravan to its destination. Nothing was simply left open, because an unresolved matter meant continuing danger. That all affairs are referred somewhere for decision was less an abstraction to that audience than a description of how their world already ran.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that all matters return to God appears several times in the Quran, and always at the end of a passage rather than at its opening. Classical commentators note the placement, since the formula works as a closing rather than a premise, marking the point where an argument has finished.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The middle ayah carries the weight of the three. After a scene of judgement, the passage states that God desires no injustice for anyone at all, which frames everything just described as the outcome of what people did rather than of what was wished on them. Placing that between the scene and the assertion of ownership keeps the ownership from being read as arbitrary power.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half of this scene, the darkened faces and the question put to them.
Says God does not wrong by the weight of an atom, and multiplies whatever is good.
Repeats the same principle in different words: God wills no injustice for the servants.

studies.applyIt: Read the middle sentence on its own: God desires no injustice for anyone. If you carry a suspicion that things are stacked against you, sit with that line for a minute rather than arguing with it. You do not have to resolve anything today. Notice only whether you actually believe it, and answer honestly.

studies.title: The Best Community And Its Conditions
studies.meaning: The superlative arrives with conditions attached. Three clauses follow it: urging good, forbidding wrong, and believing in God. Early scholars read them as the grounds of the ranking, not decoration on it. The opening verb is in the past tense. Scholars differ over whether that means the community was so in God's knowledge from the beginning, or is being reminded what it was brought out to do. The final line then refuses a blanket verdict on others.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. Much of it deals with the community's relations with the People of the Scripture there. It also deals with its recovery after the defeat at Uhud. The ayah sits in a run of passages contrasting a community held together by a shared job with one broken by rivalry. Early scholars report no single agreed occasion for it, and read it in the flow of that argument.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a mother or a source. It names a body of people bound by something they share, a direction, a calling, a moment in time, rather than by descent.
A passive verb of being drawn out or made to emerge, used elsewhere of crops pushed up from the soil. The community is not self-made; it is described as something raised for a purpose.
Literally the known, the familiar. It covers what sound human sense already recognises as decent, so the good being urged is not exotic; it is what people already acknowledge when they are honest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Medina a person's standing came from family line. Which clan, which alliance, how many fighting men could be called to a quarrel. Rank was something you inherited and defended with poetry and raids. Meccan emigrants, Medinan hosts and clans lately at war with each other were now told their rank lay in what they did, not in who they came from. That was a genuinely strange arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is bracketed by qualifications on both sides. Its own last clause says that some of the People of the Scripture believe, and three ayat later the surah states outright that they are not all alike, describing a group among them who recite through the night and prostrate. The generalisation is never left standing on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Excellence here is about function, not essence. A community is ranked by an activity it can stop doing. So the description can be lost as well as held. The order matters too. Two duties towards other people come before the mention of belief. So faith is shown leading to public duty rather than sitting apart from it. And the qualification about others keeps the claim from hardening into contempt.

crossReferences.why: States the same commission as a duty for a group within the community, a few ayat earlier.
Calls the community a middle nation set as witnesses over people, the same commissioning language.
Immediately corrects any blanket reading by naming an upright group among the People of the Scripture.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing this week that you would normally let pass: a rumour repeated in a group chat, a colleague spoken about unfairly. Say something, briefly and without heat, and then let it go. The ayah ties the community's worth to small interventions like that one, made by people who would rather have stayed quiet.
studies.explainEasier: God tells this community they are the best one raised up for people. But that comes with a job. They tell people to do good, warn them away from wrong, and believe in God.

studies.title: No Harm Beyond Insult
studies.meaning: A limit is placed on what opposition can achieve. The harm is said to reach no further than words that wound, and if it comes to fighting, the outcome is named in advance. Classical commentators read the passage as reassurance given at a particular moment rather than as a general rule about every future encounter, and they note the word chosen for the harm, which covers annoyance and injury of a kind that does not reach the vital parts.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage describing the community as raised up for the good of people. The classical commentaries place these ayat in a period of pressure from groups in and around the city, and read them as addressed to a community with real reason to feel outnumbered. The reassurance is specific to that setting, and the surah shortly afterwards turns to a battle that went badly.

keyTerms.note: A word for harm that irritates and wounds without destroying. The Quran uses it of insult, of discomfort and of minor injury, so it names a category of damage rather than a degree of it.
An idiom for fleeing, built from the word for a back. Arabic describes a retreat by what the pursuer sees, which is more vivid than the abstract word for flight would be.
The passive of the verb for coming to someone's aid, from the same root used earlier in this surah of the disciples. The passive form leaves the absent helper entirely unnamed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Insult was a weapon in Arabia, and a serious one. Satirical poetry could damage a tribe's standing for a generation, and poets were employed for exactly that purpose. Being told that opposition would go no further than words was no small reassurance to that audience. Words were the instrument they most feared after the sword, and sometimes before it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for harm appears more than twenty times in the Quran, covering things as different as verbal abuse, physical discomfort and the injury done by a boastful gift. Its range is wide enough that classical lexicographers define it partly by what it excludes: damage that does not destroy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a boundary around what opposition can do, which is different from promising that none will come. Insult and irritation are conceded outright; the claim concerns where the damage stops. That is a particular kind of comfort, since it neither denies the difficulty nor treats it as decisive, and it leaves a person free to feel the sting without concluding anything from it.

crossReferences.why: Says plainly that you will hear much hurt, and joins it to patience and mindfulness.
Tells the Prophet to disregard the hurt they cause, and to rely on God instead.
Names giving followed by no reminder and no hurt as the giving that keeps its reward.

studies.applyIt: Someone will say something to you this week that stings and changes nothing. Notice the gap between how much it hurts and how much it actually does. Those two quantities are almost never the same, and this ayah's whole comfort lies in keeping them apart. Name the second one out loud; it usually turns out to be small.

studies.title: Except By Two Ropes
studies.meaning: A condition of humiliation and hardship is described as having settled over a community in the past, and the causes are named inside the ayah itself: refusing God's signs, killing prophets, disobedience and transgression. Two exceptions are stated in the middle of it, both called ropes, one from God and one from people. Classical commentators read them as a covenant with God and a bond of protection or treaty with other human beings, so the way out is named alongside the condition.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section that alternates between description and qualification. The classical commentaries read the passage as an account of a historical condition attached to specific named conduct, not as a permanent verdict on any people. The very next ayah states directly that they are not all alike and describes an upright community among them, and the sources treat that as part of how this ayah is read.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb used of pitching a tent over a place. The image is of something set up above and around people, so the condition is described as a covering rather than as a quality they possess.
The word for a rope, used in Arabic for a covenant or a protection agreement. The same image appears a few ayat earlier in this surah, where believers are told to hold to God's rope together.
From the root that gives Arabic its word for the poor and for stillness. It names an inability to move or improve one's position rather than poverty measured as a bare quantity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection agreements were the fabric of Arabian security. A group without a treaty was exposed everywhere it went, while one with a bond could travel and trade in safety. Such agreements were spoken of as ropes and as ties, and everyone understood that the difference between a secure life and an exposed one was often a single arrangement with a stronger party.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of a rope appears twice within ten ayat of this surah, once as the rope of God that believers are told to hold to together, and once here as the exception to a described condition. The same everyday word carries a promise in one place and a way out in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah states causes rather than declaring a nature, which is what allows the following ayah to say plainly that they are not all alike. Read together, the two make a claim about how consequences work: conduct is named, its effects are described, and the description is immediately prevented from hardening into a category. The exception clauses do the same work from inside the ayah.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately and says they are not alike, describing an upright community among them.
Uses the same image of a rope from God, as what believers are to hold to together.
Describes the same condition and names the same causes, in an earlier surah's account.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the ayah names causes and then, one line later, refuses to let the description become a label. That is a discipline worth borrowing. When you find yourself explaining a whole group by a pattern, say the next sentence too: they are not all alike. Say it out loud, and mean it about a specific person you know.

studies.title: They Are Not All Alike
studies.meaning: A short clause opens the ayah and revises everything before it: they are not alike. What follows is entirely positive, a description of an upright community among the People of the Book who recite God's verses through the hours of the night and prostrate. Classical commentators note the word for upright, which describes something standing firm, and the choice of the night hours, which places the practice where nobody is watching. Nothing in the description is hedged or qualified.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after a passage describing a condition and its causes. The classical commentaries treat the placement as the point of the ayah, since it stops the preceding description from being generalised. Some sources connect it to members of the scriptural communities of Medina who had joined the young community, while others read it more broadly. The commendation itself is not disputed.

keyTerms.note: A word for evenness, used of a level surface and of two things of the same measure. Denying it says the members of a group are not interchangeable, which is a claim about internal variety.
A noun for a body of people joined to a participle meaning standing. The image is of standing firm and standing in prayer at the same time, and the commentators keep both senses in view.
A plural noun for the successive portions of the night. Naming them in the plural suggests recitation spread across the night rather than confined to one vigil at a fixed hour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night belonged to whoever chose it. Lamps were expensive, oil was rationed, and most households went dark shortly after the evening meal. Anyone reciting through the hours of darkness was spending a resource and losing sleep before a working day. It was the least visible and most costly kind of devotion, and nobody would know unless a neighbour happened to hear.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah begins one of the Quran's most direct refusals to generalise, and the passage it opens runs for three ayat of unqualified commendation. The word for community used here is the same one the surah applies a few ayat earlier to the believers themselves, which places both groups under one term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to generalise is presented as a matter of accuracy rather than of courtesy. A description of a group's conduct is followed at once by the statement that the group is not uniform, which treats even a warranted criticism as incomplete without it. The commendation that follows matters too: it is given for practices anyone would recognise as devotion, with no condition of membership attached.

crossReferences.why: Describes the condition this ayah immediately qualifies, one line earlier in the surah.
Closes the surah by describing those among the People of the Book who believe with humility.
Describes those nearest in affection to the believers, and their tears on hearing revelation.

studies.applyIt: Find one group you hold a settled opinion about, and think of a specific person inside it who does not fit. Not as a rhetorical exercise: an actual person with a name. Hold both facts at once, the pattern you noticed and the individual who contradicts it. This ayah's whole method is insisting both stay in the sentence.

studies.title: Quick To The Good
studies.meaning: The commendation continues and becomes a list: belief in God and the Last Day, urging what is recognised as right, restraining what is wrong, and hurrying toward good deeds. The verb for hurrying is the striking one, since it describes competing rather than merely doing. A guarantee follows: whatever good they do will not be denied them. Classical commentators note that these are exactly the qualities the surah applies to the believing community a few ayat earlier.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the passage that refuses to generalise about the People of the Book. These two ayat complete a description begun with an upright community reciting through the night. The classical commentaries observe that the qualities named are the same ones the surah has already applied to the believers themselves, and read the repetition as deliberate rather than incidental.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb to know. It names what a sound conscience already recognises, so the good being urged is described as familiar rather than newly imposed from outside.
The counterpart term, from a root meaning to find something strange or to deny it. Wrong is named as what the same conscience refuses, which pairs the two words as recognition and its opposite.
A form of the verb to hurry that carries competition. It describes not merely speed but eagerness measured against others, so the good is pursued rather than simply performed.
From the root meaning to cover over, used elsewhere in this surah of refusing signs. Applied to a reward it means having a deed covered up and left unacknowledged by anyone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Recognition was the currency of a small society. A man who acted well in a public matter expected it to be remembered, and a slight went unforgotten for a generation. Being denied credit for something you did was among the more corrosive injuries in that world, worse in some ways than losing property, since reputation could not be rebuilt by working harder.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs for urging the good and restraining the wrong appear together as a fixed pair throughout the Quran, and this surah applies them to the believing community a few ayat earlier. Using the identical formula here of a group among the People of the Book is one of the passage's most deliberate features.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The guarantee is attached to actions rather than to affiliation: good done will not go unacknowledged, and the doer's community is left unmentioned. Read alongside the identical description of the believers a few lines earlier, the effect is to make the qualities themselves the operative thing. The closing clause, that God knows the mindful, places the accounting beyond human sorting.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same three qualities of the believing community, a few ayat earlier in this surah.
Describes prophets racing toward good deeds and calling on God in hope and in awe.
Instructs everyone to compete in good works, wherever it is that they turn.

studies.applyIt: Pick the good thing you have been meaning to do and have kept rescheduling. The verb here is about racing, and the enemy of racing is deferral rather than laziness. Do the smaller version today rather than the better version next month, and notice how much of the delay was about wanting it to look impressive.

studies.title: Said Again, Ending Elsewhere
studies.meaning: The sentence is almost the one this surah used a hundred ayat earlier, and the difference lies at the end. There the closing image was fuel; here it is companionship, describing those addressed as the people of the Fire who remain in it. Classical commentators note that the surah repeats formulations at intervals with altered endings, and read the change as marking how far the argument has travelled between two occurrences rather than as variation without purpose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the passage commending an upright group among the People of the Book. The placement is deliberate: a warm description is followed at once by a warning, and the warning is addressed to a category defined by refusal rather than to any community. The classical commentaries treat the pairing as this surah's way of preventing either statement from being read on its own.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a close associate or a travelling companion. Arabic uses it for those permanently attached to a place or a condition, so the phrase describes belonging rather than location.
From a root meaning to persist and to endure without change. It describes duration without alteration, which is why the same word is used of both the garden and the fire in this surah.
Named with the definite article, as a known thing rather than as a description. The Quran generally uses it this way, assuming that the referent is understood rather than introducing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging in Arabia was expressed in exactly this form. A man was named as one of the people of a valley, a well or a tribe, and that phrase told you everything about where he could travel safely and who would answer for him. Being called the companions of something was a statement of identity, not of address, and the audience heard it in that register.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats an earlier one in the same surah almost word for word, changing only its closing image. Surah 3 does this several times, restating a formulation after a long stretch of intervening material, and the repetitions are one of the ways the chapter holds a long and varied argument together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing this immediately after a commendation of people outside the community does something specific. It shows that neither generosity nor warning is being distributed by group, since the preceding ayat praised without qualification and this one warns without naming anyone. What determines the outcome in both cases is described entirely in terms of conduct and refusal, which is the surah's consistent position.

crossReferences.why: States the same claim almost word for word earlier in this surah, closing on a different image.
Supplies the commendation of an upright group that this warning immediately follows.
Repeats the same formula about wealth and children availing nothing against God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how the surah alternates: praise, then warning, then praise again, never letting either settle into a verdict about a group. If you tend to read scripture looking for confirmation about who is in and who is out, this stretch is built to make that difficult. Read the four ayat around this one in order.

studies.title: A Wind With Frost In It
studies.meaning: A comparison is drawn for what is spent without anything behind it. It is like a wind carrying bitter cold that reaches a standing crop and destroys it. The detail that matters is what was lost: not seed, but a harvest, something already grown and nearly ready to cut. Classical commentators note the closing clause, which turns the loss inward. God did not wrong them; the wrong was already in the field, since the owners are described as having wronged themselves before the wind arrived.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section describing those who oppose the community. The classical commentaries connect the parable to spending done for reputation or for advantage, including expenditure on campaigns against the young community. The Quran names no occasion, and the sources treat the comparison as general, since its point concerns the relation between an act and whatever stands behind it.

keyTerms.note: A word for intense cold, from a root also connected with a persistent sound and with tying something tightly. It names cold as something that grips rather than merely as a lowered temperature.
The word for cultivated ground and what grows on it, used earlier in this surah among the things people love. It covers the labour that went in as well as the crop that came up.
The object is placed before the verb, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis. The word order insists that the wronged party and the one doing the wrong are the same people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A crop lost late was the worst kind of loss. Seed that failed cost a season's seed; a standing harvest destroyed days before cutting cost the seed, the water, the labour and the whole year's food. Frost was the specific fear on higher ground, arriving in one night without warning. Everyone farming knew families ruined in exactly that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the tilled field in this parable appears earlier in this same surah, in the list of things made attractive to people. The Quran often reuses a term across a chapter in different roles, and here one word names both something loved and something destroyed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parable locates the failure before the disaster. A wind destroys the crop, but the ayah says the wrong was already done, and done by the owners to themselves. That reframes loss as disclosure rather than as punishment: what happens reveals what the spending actually was, since an act performed for the wrong reason was never carrying what its owner believed it carried.

crossReferences.why: Compares a gift given for show to soil on a rock washed bare by heavy rain.
Compares the deeds of those who refused to ashes blown apart by wind on a stormy day.
Describes deeds turned into scattered dust once they are finally brought forward.

studies.applyIt: Think of something good you did recently and ask, honestly, what you were hoping would follow from it. Not to spoil it, and not to conclude that you should stop. Just notice the answer. This parable is about what stands behind an act, and that is usually easier to see in a small case than a large one.

studies.title: Confidants From Outside
studies.meaning: The word translated here as friends means the lining of a garment, and it names an inner circle, the people close enough to know what is not said publicly. The warning concerns admitting to that circle those who wish you harm, and the description is precise: they will not stop short of ruining you, they would like to see you strained, hostility has already surfaced in their speech, and what is concealed is greater. The passage closes by saying the signs have been made plain, if you use reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a period when the community's plans and internal affairs were of practical interest to groups actively opposed to it. The classical commentaries read the ayah as concerning confidential counsel rather than ordinary dealings, and note that the Quran elsewhere describes kindness and fairness toward those who have not fought the community. The distinction is drawn by the vocabulary itself.

keyTerms.note: The word for the inner lining of a garment, the layer that sits against the skin. Used of people it names close confidants, so the warning concerns access rather than acquaintance.
A noun covering corruption, confusion and loss of one's senses. It names damage that spoils the working of a thing rather than destroying the thing outright.
From a root meaning to be strained or brought into difficulty, used of a bone breaking after it had begun to set. It names distress arising from pressure rather than from a single blow.
An intensive form from the root for hatred. Its appearance is described as having already surfaced in speech, which is what makes the concealed portion something a listener can infer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city the size of Medina, a household's confidential business travelled at the speed of a single conversation. Plans for a journey, a marriage negotiation, a debt coming due, the movements of a caravan, all of it had value to somebody. There were no locked archives. Who you spoke freely in front of was the entire information policy available to a family or a community.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for an inner circle comes from the vocabulary of clothing, naming the lining that sits against the body, and Arabic uses its counterpart for the outer face of a garment. The pair gives the language a way of distinguishing what is close and hidden from what is put on display.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the people you deal with from the people you confide in, and places the warning only on the second. That leaves ordinary relations untouched while treating access to a community's inner deliberation as a matter of judgement rather than of goodwill. Ending on reason rather than on obedience also frames the instruction as something to be understood rather than simply followed.

crossReferences.why: Instructs kindness and fairness toward those who did not fight you over religion.
Continues immediately, describing an affection that runs in only one direction.
Uses the same word for an inner circle, in a passage about who is taken into confidence.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between who you are kind to and who you tell things to. Most people manage the first carefully and the second by accident. Think about the last thing you were genuinely worried about and who ended up hearing it. Ask whether that list was chosen, or simply whoever happened to be nearby.

studies.title: You Love Them, They Do Not
studies.meaning: An asymmetry is described, and the believers are not blamed for it. They love people who do not love them back, and they accept the whole of scripture while others do not extend the same acceptance. Then a scene in two settings: warmth when they meet, and fingers bitten in rage when they are alone. The instruction that follows is brief and uncomfortable. Classical commentators read the phrase about dying in one's rage as a statement about the futility of that anger rather than as an imprecation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the previous ayah's discussion of who is admitted to a community's confidence. The classical commentaries place these ayat among groups in Medina whose public conduct differed from their private view. Reports of specific individuals vary, so the surah keeps to the general description, as it does throughout this section, and the emphasis falls on the gap between the two settings.

keyTerms.gloss: they bit their fingertips at you
keyTerms.note: A physical idiom for rage that has found no outlet. Arabic uses it of frustration turned on the self, and the specific noun names the tips of the fingers rather than the hand.
Distinguished by the lexicographers from ordinary anger as the inward heat that has not yet been discharged. It names the feeling itself rather than any act arising out of it.
Literally the owner or substance of the chests. The construction names not merely the contents but the settled disposition beneath them, which is why translators reach for the heart.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public courtesy was obligatory in Arabian society and told you very little. Hospitality was extended to people you intended to fight, and greeting a man warmly in the market said nothing at all about what you said of him at home. Everyone understood that the two registers existed side by side. What was rare was any way of knowing which one you were actually in.
studies.didYouKnow: The gesture of biting the fingers in rage appears in the Quran in one other place, where a wrongdoer bites his hands in regret on the Day of Judgement. Both uses describe a body turning frustration on itself at a moment when nothing whatever can be done about the cause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage acknowledges an affection that is not returned without instructing anyone to withdraw it. What is corrected is not the love but the misreading of the situation, so the believers are given accurate information rather than a change of heart. The final clause moves the whole matter into God's knowledge, which is this surah's usual way of closing a description of what people conceal.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same group one ayah earlier, warning against admitting them to confidence.
Uses the same gesture of biting the hands, in regret rather than in rage.
States earlier in this surah that God knows what the chests hold, concealed or disclosed.

studies.applyIt: There is probably someone you like more than they like you. That is ordinary and not a failure on either side. This ayah does not tell the believers to stop caring; it tells them to see the situation accurately. Try holding both facts about one relationship this week, without adjusting the warmth and without pretending.

studies.title: Their Scheming Will Not Reach You
studies.meaning: A pattern is described first: your good fortune upsets them, and your misfortune pleases them. Then a condition follows, and it is not a strategy. If you endure and remain mindful, their scheming will not harm you at all. Classical commentators note that nothing is said about countering the plan; the protection offered is attached entirely to the conduct of the person threatened. The closing description says God encompasses what they do, which is a claim about scope rather than about response.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short passage about confidants and concealed hostility. The classical commentaries connect it to the period around the difficult day at Uhud, when the community's setbacks were watched closely by those hoping for them. The surah turns to that battle in the very next ayah, so this instruction sits immediately before an account of a genuine reverse.

keyTerms.note: A verb of light contact, used of one thing brushing against another. It is used here of good fortune while a stronger verb is used of misfortune, a difference the commentators notice.
A verb of hitting a target, stronger than the one used of good fortune in the same sentence. The pairing suggests that difficulty arrives with more force than ease ever does.
A noun for a plan laid quietly, from a root also used of straining and of a trick. It names the arrangement itself rather than any act eventually carried out through it.
An active participle from the verb to surround, used of a wall enclosing a place. It describes knowledge as containment, so nothing done is outside the perimeter of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where everyone's fortunes were public, the pleasure taken in a rival's setback was a recognised social fact. A failed harvest, a lost caravan or a marriage broken off was discussed everywhere within days. There was no privacy in which to fail. Living well under that kind of observation was a practical problem people faced constantly.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs used in this ayah for good and bad fortune are deliberately unequal in force, one meaning to touch lightly and the other to strike a target. The Quran uses this asymmetry in several places, and classical commentators read it as reflecting how differently the two are actually experienced.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The protection offered is conditional on the conduct of the one threatened rather than on any action taken against the threat. That relocates security from the outcome of a contest into the state of the person exposed, which is a substantial claim: what makes a scheme harmless is described as happening in the target, not in the plan. The closing name keeps the scheme visible without letting it be decisive.

crossReferences.why: Joins the same two qualities, patience and mindfulness, to hearing much hurt from others.
Says God does not guide the scheming of the treacherous through to its intended end.
States that an evil scheme encircles only the people who devise it.

studies.applyIt: Someone is probably pleased about a setback of yours right now. You cannot do anything about that, and trying to is precisely what this ayah declines to recommend. Instead, name the two things it does ask for, endurance and mindfulness, and pick the smaller of the two to work on today.

studies.title: The Morning You Went Out
studies.meaning: The account of the hard day begins not with the fighting but with a morning: leaving home and assigning positions. Then two admissions in quick succession. Two groups among the believers almost lost heart, and the ayah says God was their protector in that very moment. Then a reminder of the earlier victory, won when the community was weak, and an instruction that closes on thankfulness. Classical commentators note that the passage opens its account of a defeat by recalling a victory.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's long treatment of the battle at Uhud in the third year after the migration. A force from Mecca came to avenge its losses at Badr, and the Muslim force met it outside the city. The classical sources agree on the broad course of the day, including the near-withdrawal of two groups before the fighting, which the Quran records here without softening it.

keyTerms.gloss: you set out in the morning
keyTerms.note: A verb specific to the early part of the day, from the root that gives Arabic its word for tomorrow. The time of day is built into the verb rather than added on beside it.
From a root meaning to settle someone in a place, used of finding lodging for a traveller. Applied to a battle line it means putting each group where it is meant to stay.
A dual verb from a root covering weakness of resolve and failure of nerve. The dual form is exact, naming two groups and no more, which is why the report cannot be generalised.
The plural of a word for one who is lowly or without power. Used of the earlier battle it concedes the community's own weakness rather than describing anything about its opponents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A battle in that world was decided before contact as often as during it. Position, high ground and the discipline of holding a line mattered more than numbers, and a force that broke formation was usually finished. Men fought beside relatives, so a single group withdrawing exposed families as well as flanks. Assigning positions in the morning was the most consequential work of the day.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names the earlier battle of Badr directly in this passage, one of very few places where it names a battlefield at all. Most of its references to specific events describe them without naming them, which makes the explicit naming here, inside an account of a later and harder day, unusually direct.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The most striking clause is the one about the two groups who nearly faltered, since it says God was their protector in the same breath. Failure of nerve is recorded and not disowned, and the relationship is not described as suspended by it. That establishes something the rest of the Uhud section develops: the account can be honest about weakness because the argument does not depend on denying it.

crossReferences.why: Recalls Badr earlier in this surah, describing the two parties and the sign in them.
Describes the appeal for help at Badr and the reinforcement sent as reassurance.
Continues this account, describing the moment the line broke and giving the reason.

studies.applyIt: Notice the shape of this opening: before describing a bad day it recalls a good one, and the weakness that preceded that. When something goes wrong this week, try beginning your account of it in the same place, with what went right before and how thin the margin actually was. It changes what the difficult part means.

studies.title: Three Thousand Sent Down
studies.meaning: A question is quoted rather than a statement made: is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforces you with three thousand angels sent down. Classical commentators differ over which battle the number belongs to, some reading it of the earlier day at Badr and others of the encounter this passage describes, and the sources record the disagreement without settling it. What is not in dispute is the form. Reassurance is offered as a question, which leaves the hearer to answer.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the account of the battle at Uhud, though the classical commentaries differ over whether the promise reported here belongs to that day or to the earlier victory at Badr. Both readings are preserved in the major commentaries along with their evidence. The Quran does not resolve it, and the surah moves straight on to a conditional promise of further reinforcement.

keyTerms.note: From the root for sufficiency, the same one behind the phrase God is enough for us that appears later in this surah. It asks about adequacy rather than about what anyone wants.
From a root meaning to stretch or extend, used of a supply line and of ink drawn from a well. Help is pictured as something extended outward rather than simply dropped in.
A passive participle stressing that the reinforcement descends rather than merely arrives. The commentators note that the same root runs through this surah's vocabulary for revelation itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Numbers in Arabian warfare were known and counted. Before an engagement, scouts reported the opposing force and men made their own calculations about whether to stand. Three thousand was a figure larger than most armies the peninsula had ever assembled, so naming it named a quantity outside ordinary experience while still using the terms a fighter would think in.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives specific numbers of angels in only a small number of places, and two of them concern battles fought by this community. Elsewhere angelic presence is described with no figure at all, which makes the counted reinforcements in this surah and in Surah 8 unusual within the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Offering reassurance as a question puts the work of belief on the hearer rather than delivering a guarantee. It also frames unseen help as already given rather than promised, since the verb describes reinforcement already under way. The passage therefore meets fear by supplying information about the present instead of about the outcome, which is a different kind of comfort from a prediction.

crossReferences.why: Describes the appeal at Badr and a thousand angels sent in succession as the answer.
Raises the number conditionally in the very next ayah, on two stated conditions.
Speaks of forces nobody could see, sent down at a moment when numbers had failed.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this is a question. When you are afraid you probably ask for reassurance and rarely stop to answer whether what you already have would be enough. Try that today with one specific worry: list what you actually have in hand, then answer the question honestly instead of moving straight on to asking for more.

studies.title: If You Hold And Guard
studies.meaning: The answer to the previous question arrives in one word meaning on the contrary, and the promise is then extended with conditions attached. If you hold fast, if you remain mindful, and if they come upon you suddenly, the reinforcement rises to five thousand marked angels. Classical commentators discuss the word describing them, which suggests distinguishing marks, and preserve more than one explanation. The conditions are the notable part, since unseen help is described as tied to what the people receiving it do.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of the battle at Uhud and its promise of reinforcement. The classical commentaries differ over whether the promised five thousand were sent, since many read the attached conditions as having gone unmet on that day. The sources preserve the discussion carefully, and the surah's later account of the battle describes exactly the failure of resolve those conditions concern.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to boil over, used of water and of a sudden surge. It describes an attack arriving at once and without pause, which is why translators reach for the word suddenly.
An active participle from the root for marking, the same one used earlier in this surah of branded horses. Commentators explain it variously as marked in appearance or as marking their targets.
From the root covering binding and restraint. In a battle setting it names holding a position under pressure, which is exactly what the surah's later account says was not done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Discipline decided engagements in that world. A line that held under archery could win against greater numbers; a line that moved to collect plunder lost the field. Commanders repeated their position orders because everyone knew how quickly a formation dissolved once men began thinking individually. The conditions in this ayah are stated in the vocabulary of exactly that problem.
studies.didYouKnow: The number in this ayah rises from the one before it, three thousand to five thousand, and the increase arrives with conditions the earlier figure did not carry. Classical commentators treat the conditional structure as significant, and much of their discussion concerns whether the larger reinforcement was in fact ever sent.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches unseen assistance to human conduct without making it a payment for it. Endurance and mindfulness are named as conditions rather than as causes, and the help remains God's to extend. That holds together two things easily separated: the assurance that support exists, and the seriousness of what a person actually does while waiting for it to arrive.

crossReferences.why: Asks the question this ayah answers, about whether the first reinforcement would suffice.
Describes the moment later in this surah when holding fast gave way, and what followed.
Ties a promised advantage in battle to the state of the people receiving it.

studies.applyIt: The two conditions here are endurance and care. Both are unglamorous, and both are practised in advance rather than summoned in the moment. Pick one situation you know is coming and decide now, in writing if it helps, what holding your position will actually look like when it arrives.

studies.title: Only Good News For You
studies.meaning: The purpose of the reinforcement is stated plainly, and it is not military. God made it good news for you, and so that your hearts would settle. Then the point is made without hedging: help comes only from God. Classical commentators read this as correcting a natural misunderstanding, since a promise of thousands of angels invites the thought that the numbers are doing the work. The ayah says the numbers were for the hearts, and the outcome was never a matter of counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about angelic reinforcement inside the account of the battle. The classical commentaries treat this ayah as the interpretive key to the two before it, since it states what the promise was actually for. The surah's larger argument about the day is being set up here, because the community's confidence had to be located somewhere other than in a visible advantage.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind announcing glad tidings and the visible change in a face at good news. It names the message rather than the thing announced, which is precisely the distinction the ayah draws.
From a root describing ground that is level and still, and a heart at rest. It pictures reassurance as settling rather than as excitement, a quieter image than the English usually suggests.
From the root for coming to someone's aid, the same one used of the disciples earlier in this surah. It names assistance given, so victory is described as something received rather than achieved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Morale was understood as a material factor in Arabian warfare. Commanders spread reports of allies coming, of reinforcements on the road, of an enemy's losses, because a force that believed itself supported fought differently from one that did not. Everyone knew that what men believed about their numbers mattered as much as the numbers themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying victory comes only from God appears twice in the Quran, here and in Surah 8, both times inside an account of a battle and both times immediately after a mention of angelic reinforcement. The repetition in such closely matched settings is among the tightest parallels between those two surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates a cause from a comfort. Thousands of angels are described as given for the sake of the hearts rather than as the mechanism of the outcome, which stops unseen help from being counted as a resource. That guards against two errors at once: relying on visible strength, and relying on invisible strength as though it were the same kind of thing.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing in nearly identical words, after the reinforcement at Badr.
Says later in this surah that if God helps you, no one at all can overcome you.
Names what hearts actually settle by, which is the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice the distinction between what actually does the work and what was given to steady you. Most reassurance is of the second kind, and mistaking it for the first is how people end up disappointed in things that were never load-bearing. Ask which of your current supports is which, and be honest about one of them.

studies.title: None Of It Is Yours To Decide
studies.meaning: Two purposes are named for what happens in a battle, and they are offered as alternatives: to cut off a portion of those who refuse, or to subdue them so they turn back with nothing. Then the address turns personal and sets a limit. None of the matter is yours, whether God turns to them in mercy or punishes them. Classical commentators report an occasion in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), wounded and grieving, had begun to name particular opponents in supplication against them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the account of the battle at Uhud, in which the community suffered heavy losses including close relatives of many present. The classical commentaries report that the Prophet began naming opponents in supplication and that this ayah followed. Several of those named are reported to have joined the community later, which the sources note as bearing directly on how the ayah is read.

keyTerms.note: The word for the extremity of a thing, a limb or a border. Cutting off an edge describes a partial reduction rather than a destruction, which is what the alternative in the ayah offers.
A verb for humbling someone through frustration, connected with grief and with turning back thwarted. It names the defeat of an intention rather than the defeat of a force.
A participle from the root for a failed venture, used of a hunt that returns with nothing. It describes the state of someone whose whole effort produced no return at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cursing an enemy by name was a recognised practice, and a man wronged in battle was expected to invoke against those who had wronged him. Poets composed such invocations formally, and communities repeated them for years. To be told, in the middle of a day of losses, that the matter was not yours at all ran directly against what grief in that culture was permitted to do.
studies.didYouKnow: The limit set in this passage is placed in the middle of a sentence, so the clause about mercy or punishment interrupts a description of what God does in battle. Classical commentators note that the interruption is itself the point, since the instruction arrives inside an account of the very day that provoked it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes the final verdict from the person with the strongest claim to want it. Someone wounded and bereaved is told that the outcome for his opponents is not his concern in either direction, mercy or punishment. That leaves grief its full weight while denying it any authority, and the later history of some of those involved suggests why the door was kept open.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately, stating that God forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.
Tells the Prophet his duty is to convey, and that the reckoning belongs to God.
Repeats the same limit: you are a reminder, and not one set in control over them.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who has genuinely wronged you, and notice how much of your inner argument is about what should happen to them. This passage does not ask you to forgive them or to stop hurting. It removes the verdict from your hands, which is different, and often more of a relief than forgiveness would be.

studies.title: Forgives Whom He Wills
studies.meaning: The limit set in the previous ayah is grounded in a statement of ownership. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, so the disposal of it is His. Then two clauses in perfect balance: He forgives whom He wills, He punishes whom He wills. The ayah does not leave them balanced, though. It closes on two names drawn from the vocabulary of mercy, which the early scholars read as tilting the sentence without cancelling either half of it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It comes straight after the ayah saying that the outcome for the Prophet's opponents is not his to decide. The early scholars read the two ayat as one argument. A limit is placed on a man, and then the reason is given. The ayah belongs to the account of the battle at Uhud. Its content is general, though, and the tradition quotes it on its own.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cover, the same one behind the Arabic word for a helmet. Forgiveness is described as covering a thing rather than as erasing it, a different picture from the English.
An intensive form of the same root, describing not a single act but a settled and repeated disposition. Its placement at the end of the ayah is what gives the whole sentence its direction.
The second of the two closing names, from the root shared with the word for a womb. Paired with the first, it joins the covering of faults to an active and persisting compassion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ownership settled everything in Arabian life. A man could do as he liked with his own camels, his own well and his own land. Nobody asked him about it. Claims and disputes were nearly always arguments about who owned a thing, not about who could use it. So a statement about God's freedom, grounded in ownership, spoke in the plainest terms the audience had.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close this ayah appear together more than seventy times in the Quran. No other pair of divine names is joined that often. They nearly always come at the end of an ayah rather than at its start. They close a passage rather than open one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah states two outcomes in the same shape, then breaks the match with the names at the end. That is built on purpose.
