Nothing here is promised to anyone, and yet the sentence does not stop halfway. Grounding it in ownership matters too. It makes both mercy and punishment come from one fact about God, not from two moods pulling against each other.

crossReferences.why: Sets the limit this ayah explains, that the outcome is not the Prophet's to determine.
Answers a claim to privileged standing with the same statement of ownership and will.
States the widest form of the mercy this ayah's closing names point toward.

studies.applyIt: Read the two halves of this ayah aloud and notice that they are the same length and shape, then notice where the sentence actually ends. That ending is a choice the text makes. When you next find yourself running through what someone deserves, put the closing clause where the text puts it and stop there.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. He can forgive anyone He chooses, and He can punish anyone He chooses. The ayah ends by calling Him the One who forgives again and again.

studies.title: Doubled And Doubled Again
studies.meaning: The address is to believers, and the practice named is lending at an increase that piles up: a debt doubled, then doubled again on top of the doubling. The early scholars describe the exact form meant here. A debtor who could not pay on time had the sum raised and the deadline pushed back. A small loan could then grow past any hope of repayment. The two ayat after it set the instruction inside something larger. They tie being mindful of God, and obeying, to the hope of mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, set inside the account of the battle at Uhud. The early scholars treat that placing as deliberate, not accidental. A community that had just been through loss and division is addressed about how its members deal with each other's money. The practice named was ordinary in Arabian trade. This surah treats it only briefly, since a much longer treatment comes in an earlier surah.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to grow or swell, used of a hill rising out of a plain. The word names the increase itself rather than the lending, which is why the Quran describes it by what it does.
A noun paired with a participle from its own root, so the phrase doubles the idea of doubling. The sound of it performs the compounding that the sense is describing.
From a root meaning to split open, used of a farmer breaking the earth. Success in Arabic is pictured as cutting through to what lies underneath rather than as accumulation on top.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Credit ran everything in Mecca and Medina, and there were no courts to restructure a debt. A man who could not pay at term negotiated with whoever held the loan, and the usual terms were more time in exchange for a larger sum. Families lost land, and sometimes their freedom, through exactly that sequence. Everyone had watched a neighbour disappear into it.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah handles the subject briefly, inside a passage about a battle. A much longer treatment sits near the end of Surah 2. The early scholars discuss how the two relate. Part of what they weigh is the placing here, among ayat about loss and division inside the community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction sits between two ayat that widen it a long way. One warns about guarding against the Fire. The other joins obedience to the hope of mercy. That frame treats money as part of the same life as everything else, not as a separate department. The setting inside a hard battle adds a further point. How a community deals with its own members bears on how it stands outside.

crossReferences.why: Treats the same subject at length, including the instruction to grant a struggling debtor time.
Contrasts what is given to grow among people's wealth with what is given seeking God's face.
Describes a loan given to God instead, and multiplied many times over.

studies.applyIt: This passage puts money inside a chapter about loss, division and mercy. That suggests they belong together. Take one money arrangement you are part of. Ask what it does to the relationship around it. Not whether it is allowed. Just what it does to the two people in it.
studies.explainEasier: Do not lend money and keep piling more and more onto what someone owes you. Be careful of God instead, and stay away from the Fire. Do what God and the Messenger say, and you may be shown mercy.

studies.title: The Race And Its Runners
studies.meaning: A command to hurry is followed by a description of the people who arrive, and it is not a list of heroics. Giving when money is easy and when it is not. Swallowing anger while it is still hot. Pardoning people who are in the wrong. Early scholars note the sequence: restraint comes before pardon, because holding the anger in is the step that makes forgiving possible. The reward named first is forgiveness, not the Garden.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This sits in the long section that works through the defeat at Uhud and what came after. The ayat just before it warn against piling up interest. The ones just after describe people who sin, remember God, and do not keep at it. So the passage sits in a stretch about a community handling its own failures, in money and in war, not one describing an untested piety.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of filling a waterskin to the top and tying it shut. The anger is not absent; it is contained, with the strain of containment part of what the word carries.
Not displeasure but the heat itself, the anger felt before anything is said or done. Naming it separately from the response shows the feeling is not what is being criticised.
A form of the verb that implies competition with others rather than mere speed. The image is a field of runners, which is why the objects raced towards are pardon and a garden, not a task.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In tribal Arabia an insult unanswered was a debt. Honour worked like credit. A slight had to be repaid, often with interest, and a man who let one pass could find his household treated as fair game. Feuds ran for generations over a wounded camel or a line of verse. Praising the person who absorbs an offence and gives nothing back turned the whole social sum upside down.
studies.didYouKnow: The width of the Garden is given in almost the same words in one other place, at 57:21. There the phrase uses the singular heaven rather than the plural used here. Both open with a command to race. In both, the width comes before any description of what is inside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures piety by what a person does with their own resentment and their own money, in good times and bad. That puts the moral test inside ordinary temper rather than in rare circumstance. The closing clause shifts the frame again. The qualities are not listed as entry requirements so much as a description of people God loves. That makes the Garden sound less like a wage and more like a place such people belong.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same image of racing towards forgiveness and a garden of that width, in a Medinan surah.
Names forgiving while angry as a mark of those who answer their Lord.
Continues the list into those who sin, seek forgiveness, and do not persist knowingly.

studies.applyIt: The next time anger rises at home, try holding it for the length of one slow breath before you answer. You are not pretending it is absent. You are testing whether the sentence you would have said is the one you actually want to have said. Notice what changes in the gap.
studies.explainEasier: Hurry towards God's forgiveness and a garden as wide as the sky and the earth. It is for people who give when things are good and when they are hard. They hold their anger in and forgive others.

studies.title: They Remember And Ask
studies.meaning: These are people who fail and then do one particular thing. They have done something indecent, or wronged themselves. They remember God and ask Him to forgive them. A question then breaks into the sentence, and it answers itself: who forgives sins but God. The last clause carries a lot of weight for the early scholars. They do not keep at what they did, and they know what they are doing. Failure is taken for granted here. What is described is the shape of the recovery, not the avoidance of the fall.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the passage that describes people who are mindful of God. It comes straight after the call to race toward forgiveness. The early scholars note where it falls: inside the surah's account of a battle in which the community had really failed. They read it as spoken to people who were, at that moment, going back over their own conduct.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to exceed proper bounds, used of anything gross or beyond measure. It names a serious wrong, and it is paired here with the milder phrase about wronging oneself.
The same verb used across the Quran for remembrance of God. Placing it as the first response to a wrong makes recollection the hinge, coming before any resolve about the future is formed.
From a root suggesting tying tightly and a persistent sound. It names holding to something stubbornly, so the denial concerns continuation rather than any repetition after a lapse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a small town there was nowhere private to fail. A wrong was known, talked about and remembered. The usual answer was to defend yourself. Admitting a fault cost your family its standing as well as your own. So owning up, instead of explaining yourself, cut against every social pressure of that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The question in the middle of this ayah, asking who forgives sins but God, cuts into a description of people to say something about God. The Quran breaks in like this elsewhere too. The early scholars note that the sentence then picks up again as if nothing had interrupted it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The portrait of a mindful person is built around failure, not around a clean record. What marks these people out is an order of steps: remember, ask, and do not dig in. The closing phrase, that they know, is demanding. It rules out keeping at a wrong and blaming it on not knowing. What is asked for is honest recognition of the fault.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same people immediately before, racing toward forgiveness and restraining anger.
Says whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness will find God forgiving.
Addresses those who have gone furthest, telling them not to despair of God's mercy.

studies.applyIt: The order here is worth copying: remember, ask, stop. Most people run it backwards. They resolve to stop first and never reach the remembering. Next time you catch yourself in something, name God before you promise anything about the future. Then see whether the promise comes out different.
studies.explainEasier: When these people do something wrong, they think of God and ask Him to forgive them. Nobody else can forgive sins. And once they know a thing is wrong, they do not keep on doing it.

studies.title: The Reward Of The Workers
studies.meaning: The reward comes in two parts, and the first is a surprise: forgiveness from their Lord, before any garden is mentioned. The early scholars note that order. A reward list that opens with pardon assumes there was something to pardon. Then comes the familiar picture of gardens with rivers, and a closing line of praise for the reward of those who work. That last word counts. They are called workers, not the righteous and not the believers, which ties the reward to effort.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the description of the mindful that began with the call to race toward forgiveness. The early scholars place the passage inside the surah's treatment of the battle at Uhud. The community had just failed, and it is now described in words that start with pardon. That setting shapes how the sources read the order of the two halves.

keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to cover, so forgiveness is pictured as something laid over a fault rather than as its erasure. Naming it first makes the fault part of the passage's assumption.
A verb of praise used only in exclamations, with no ordinary indicative sense at all. Arabic reserves it for commendation, so the clause it opens is entirely an expression of approval.
The active participle from the ordinary verb for doing and working. It names people by their labour rather than by their belief, which is a notable choice at the close of this description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A worker was paid at the end of a job, and the whole relationship rested on that moment. Harvest work, caravan work and building were all settled on completion. People talked about a generous employer for years afterwards. The line of praise that closes this ayah is the kind of thing said about a man who paid more than expected. The first listeners heard it that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about gardens with rivers running beneath them appears more than thirty times in the Quran. This surah alone holds several of them. The chapters they sit in were revealed years apart, and what surrounds the phrase changes a little each time. It is one of the most familiar patterns in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting forgiveness first in a list of rewards says something about who the reward is for. These are not people who never failed. They are people who handled failure in a certain way. So pardon is what they need first, and it is named first. Calling them workers at the end keeps effort in the picture. It does not let effort become the whole basis of what they are given.

crossReferences.why: Describes the people this reward is promised to, and what they do after a wrong.
Uses the same exclamation about the reward of those who work, at the end of a scene.
Describes the same gardens in more detail, with rivers of different kinds beneath them.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the first item on this list is being forgiven, not being rewarded. If you have been holding yourself to a standard where mistakes disqualify you, the order here is worth sitting with. Read the ayah before this one and this one together, in that order, and see what they treat as normal.
studies.explainEasier: These are the people God forgives. He gives them gardens with rivers running under them, and they stay there for good. The ayah ends by saying how fine a reward that is for people who work.

studies.title: Patterns That Have Run Before
studies.meaning: The word rendered ways means settled patterns. The instruction is to go and look at where they ended. History is treated as evidence, not as comfort. Then the address turns inward. The two bans are against sagging and against grief, in that order. The promise of being uppermost is made conditional on faith, not on numbers. Early scholars read the condition as the whole point.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This part of it addresses the community after the reverse at Uhud, in the third year after the migration. Some seventy Muslims were killed there, and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was wounded. Early scholars read these ayat as spoken into that particular grief. A defeat had happened, and the question was what to conclude from it.

keyTerms.note: A path worn by repeated use. The plural here refers to regular patterns in how communities rise and fall, treating history as something with recognisable grain rather than as a sequence of accidents.
From a root for feebleness and slackening, used of a rope losing tension or bone growing frail. The prohibition is not against feeling weak but against letting the slackness settle.
Counsel aimed at softening rather than informing. It names the kind of speech that works on the will, which is why the same sentence separates it from plain guidance and clear statement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The instruction to travel and look was practical advice, not metaphor. Meccan caravans ran north to Syria past abandoned rock-cut dwellings at al-Hijr and south to Yemen past ruined dams and dead towns. Traders knew these places as landmarks, camped near them, and told stories about them at night. A merchant hearing this ayah could name the sites he had already walked through.
studies.didYouKnow: Three different words for the same revelation appear in a single short ayah: a clear statement for all people, guidance, and counsel for those mindful of God. The audience narrows across the three. Early scholars note the movement. What reaches everyone as information becomes guidance, and then counsel, only for those who bring something to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: History is offered as a kind of evidence, open to anyone willing to go and look. That puts part of the case for revelation outside the text itself. The comfort that follows is unusual in what it does not say. It does not promise that the loss will be reversed or explained. It attaches the claim of being uppermost to a condition. So the reassurance stays honest about where the community actually stood.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately, explaining the defeat as days alternated between people rather than as abandonment.
Repeats the instruction to travel and inspect what became of stronger civilisations.
Pairs the same two words, going slack and being uppermost, in a later Medinan surah.

studies.applyIt: Think of one setback from this year that you have quietly filed as proof that you are not up to something. Write down what actually happened, in two sentences, without the conclusion attached. Then notice how much of your discouragement came from the event and how much from the verdict you added to it.
studies.explainEasier: Other peoples lived before you and their stories ended. Travel and look at what happened to them. Do not go weak and do not be sad. If you truly believe, you will come out on top.

studies.title: Days We Turn Between People
studies.meaning: The comfort here compares rather than soothes. A wound reached you, and a wound like it reached them. Then comes a rule, carried by a verb used of passing a thing from hand to hand. Days are turned about among people, and no group holds them for good. Two purposes are named for that turning. One is about what becomes known, the other about who is taken. The early scholars note that the knowing is not God learning something. It is a state being brought into the open.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's account of the battle at Uhud. The community had won at Badr and lost here. The early scholars read the comparison as aimed at the shock of a setback that follows a win, which was harder to take than a plain defeat. The passage answers it by making the turning of such days the normal thing.

keyTerms.note: A word for an open wound, from a root also connected with hardship and with something breaking the skin. It names the injury rather than the defeat, which keeps the comparison physical.
From a root meaning to pass something around in turns, which later gave Arabic its word for a state. It pictures days circulating between people rather than being awarded to anyone.
The same word this surah uses for those who testify. Its double sense joins the one who bears witness to the one who dies doing so, and the Arabic holds both at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fortune in the peninsula plainly went in circles. A tribe on top in one generation was cut down in the next by drought, a lost caravan or a defeat. The same families rose again ten years later. Nobody expected it to last, and the family histories kept the memory of both. The picture of days passed round like a bowl at a gathering needed no explaining.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for turning days about among people comes from a root that later gave Arabic its everyday word for a state or a government. The link is not an accident. Both name something that changes hands. The early Arabic dictionary writers treat that turning as the root's basic sense.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a defeat inside a pattern without explaining it away. Such days turn about, so the setback is not treated as favour being taken back. What the turning is said to do is show something. What could not be told apart before becomes plain. That makes hardship a time when things come clear, not a time of correction, and that is a different account of why it happens.

crossReferences.why: Names the second purpose immediately: to refine those who believe and to wear away refusal.
Asks whether you supposed you would enter the garden without what came to those before.
Says the same thing plainly: We will test you until the strivers and the steadfast are known.

studies.applyIt: Notice the comparison the ayah opens with. It does not say your wound is small; it says the other side is wounded too. That is a specific kind of comfort, and it works better than most. Next time you are hurt by something, ask honestly what it cost the other party. The answer is rarely nothing.
studies.explainEasier: If you have been hurt, the other side has been hurt too. Days like this are turned round between people, and nobody keeps the good ones for ever. God is letting it show who really trusts Him.

studies.title: You Wished For This
studies.meaning: Three short ayat press hard. The first names two effects of hard days, refining one group and wearing away another. The second asks whether the garden was expected without God distinguishing those who strive and those who hold fast. The third is the sharpest: you used to wish for death before you met it, and now you have seen it with your own eyes. The early scholars connect the last to those who had urged going out to meet the attacking force.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the battle at Uhud. The classical sources say that going out to meet the attacking force was urged by younger men who had missed the earlier battle and wanted the same chance. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) would rather have stayed inside the city. The sources agree that the majority view won.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of purifying gold and of removing what has been mixed in. It describes a process that takes away rather than adds, which is why it suits an account of a costly day.
From a root used of the waning moon losing its light. It names gradual erasure rather than sudden destruction, and it is paired here with the verb for refining metal.
A verb for wishing and for picturing something desirable. It names desire directed at what is not present, which is exactly what the ayah then contrasts with having seen it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Young men in Arabia grew up on poetry about courage and on the names of relatives who had fought. Missing a famous battle was a shame that followed you. The wish to be tested was real, and it formed early. What the wish meant was learned once, in a single afternoon, and the men who learned it were often barely grown.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs in the first of these ayat come from different worlds. One is used of refining metal. The other is used of the moon losing its light. Set in one short sentence, they put a cleaning process beside a shrinking one. The roots alone carry the whole contrast.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage will not let entry into the garden be taken for granted. It says the sorting must happen, and it puts that sorting in events rather than in what people say. The third ayah adds something harder. Wishing for a thing and living through it are not the same. The gap between them is not called a failure. It is what being tested means.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question, whether you expected the garden without what came to those before.
Asks whether people supposed they would be left alone on saying that they believe.
Describes what actually happened on the day this passage is referring to.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have said you wished for that would be genuinely hard: more responsibility, a test of your patience, a chance to prove something. Sit for a moment with what it would actually involve on a Tuesday afternoon. The ayah is not mocking the wish. It is asking you to know what you asked for.
studies.explainEasier: God will show who really believes and who does not. You cannot expect to walk into the garden before you are tested. Some of you wished for death before you met it. Now you have seen it close up.

studies.title: Only A Messenger
studies.meaning: A rumour ran through the battlefield that the Prophet had been killed. The answer is a statement about what a messenger is. Muhammad (peace be upon him) is a messenger, and messengers have passed away before him. Then the question: if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels. The early scholars note that the ayah does not deny grief. It separates the man from the message. And it names the other path exactly: turning round, not losing belief.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, tied to the battle at Uhud. A cry went up there that the Prophet had been killed, and part of the force gave way. The classical sources agree on the incident. They also report this ayah being recited in public at his death some years later, when the community could hardly accept it, and they describe the effect it had.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to become empty or to pass by, used of times gone and of places vacated. It describes earlier messengers as having gone before rather than as having failed at anything.
An idiom for reversing direction, built from the word for a heel. It pictures retreat as walking back the way you came, and the surah uses the same phrase again a few ayat later.
From the root for gratitude. Closing an ayah about a leader's death with a promise to the thankful is unexpected, and commentators read it as naming the response that holds when a support is removed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe often held together because of one man. When a chief fell, alliances broke up, followers scattered, and a whole confederation could be gone within a season. People expected that, and the opposing force at Uhud was counting on it. So the question this ayah asks was not for effect. It described what usually happened.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical sources report this ayah being read aloud at the moment the Prophet died. They describe the people there hearing it as if for the first time. Almost no other reading of the Quran, outside the setting where it came down, is reported this widely.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the lasting power of a message somewhere other than in the man who carried it. That claim reaches a long way. It also uses the gentlest words available for giving up: turning on the heels is about movement, not belief, so what is at stake is how people act under shock. The closing promise is made to the thankful, not to the steady, which puts the response in a different key.

crossReferences.why: States the same fact plainly: you will die, and they will die.
Follows immediately, saying no soul dies except by God's leave at an appointed term.
Asks whether, if the Prophet dies, those addressed imagine they will remain.

studies.applyIt: Consider what in your religious life depends on a particular person: a teacher, a friend who keeps you honest, a community leader. Now imagine that person gone. This is not morbid; it is the question the ayah asks directly. Identify one practice you would want to keep, and start doing it without reference to them this week.
studies.explainEasier: Muhammad is only a messenger, and messengers came and died before him. Some people would turn back the way they came if he died. That would not hurt God at all. God pays back people who are thankful.

studies.title: Death At A Written Time
studies.meaning: Two claims are set side by side. Death happens by permission and at a term already written, so it cannot be brought forward by courage or postponed by caution. Then the reward clause: whoever wants this world's return is given some of it, and whoever wants the next is given from that. The sentence then adds a third clause that does not follow the pattern of the other two, a reward for the grateful, named without limit.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This comes from the review of the battle of Uhud, in the third year after the migration. During the fighting a cry went up that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been killed, and part of the army broke. These ayat address that moment directly. Early scholars read the opening line as answering the fear that made men run.

keyTerms.note: The word used in commerce for a debt with a fixed due date. Applying it to a lifespan casts death as an appointment already entered in a ledger, not an event awaiting a cause.
From a root meaning to come back. A reward described as something that returns to the one who sent it out, which is why the same word covers both the worldly and the lasting kind.
A participle, naming a settled disposition rather than an act. It closes an ayah about wanting, suggesting the third option is not a different want but a different relation to whatever arrives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Medina and Mecca was recorded with a named term, and the whole trading world turned on those dates. A caravan financed in spring against repayment when it returned. A marriage payment deferred. A settlement due at the next harvest. Everyone knew the difference between money owed now and money owed on a date. The ayah borrows that vocabulary for the span of a life.
studies.didYouKnow: The same division of wants appears at 42:20, in a farming image rather than a trading one. There the two aims are called harvests, and the one who wants the lasting harvest has his increased. Reading the two together shows the Quran restating one point. It uses the vocabulary of whichever audience it is addressing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fixing the term of death removes risk as a reason for calculation. If the moment is already set, caution buys nothing and courage costs nothing. What remains to be decided is only what a person was aiming at. The passage then makes the aim, rather than the outcome, the thing that is answered. Gratitude is added as a separate category. That suggests it is not one more thing to want but a way of holding whatever comes.

crossReferences.why: States the same division of aims in the imagery of sowing and harvest.
Spells out what happens to the one who wants the fleeting life and the one who works for the next.
Repeats that God defers no soul once its term has come.

studies.applyIt: Take one decision you have been avoiding because of what it might cost you. Ask a narrower question than usual: what am I actually aiming at here. Say the answer out loud. Most hesitation dresses itself up as prudence. The ayah is interested in the aim underneath, not in the risk on the surface.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody dies before the time God has set. If you want only what this world gives, you get some of it. If you want what comes after, you get some of that too.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: They Did Not Weaken
studies.meaning: The ayah opens with how many, and never gives a count. Prophets before this one fought beside large companies of devoted people. Three things are then denied of them in a row. They did not lose heart at what struck them. They did not weaken. They did not give in. The verbs get more physical as they go. The early scholars discuss the rare word used for those who fought alongside them, read either as great numbers or as the learned and devoted.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the battle at Uhud and what came after it, when part of the force had given way. The passage answers the shock by setting that day inside a much longer history. Communities before this one met the same thing and did not break. The early scholars read it as comfort and correction given together, with no individual named at all.

keyTerms.note: An expression for an indefinite large number, more emphatic than the ordinary word for many. It leaves the count open, which is what makes the precedent feel long rather than specific.
A rare word the lexicographers explain variously as large numbers or as those devoted to the Lord. The Quran uses it only here, and the commentaries preserve the whole range of readings.
From a root suggesting stillness and lowering oneself. It names the visible posture of surrender rather than the inward state, which is why it comes last in the sequence of three.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A beaten force in Arabia showed it by posture as much as by words. Men sat down, laid their arms aside, sent out a delegate. Everyone knew the signs. The three denials in this ayah move from the inward to the visible, ending with the posture itself. The first listeners followed that as a description of the stages of giving up.
studies.didYouKnow: The rare word this ayah uses for those who fought beside the earlier prophets is found nowhere else in the Quran. Words that appear only once form a known category in the classical scholarly writing. They draw long discussion for a simple reason. There is no second use to compare them with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comfort offered is history, not a promise. Nothing is said about how things will turn out. What is said is that others stood where you stand and held. Closing on God's love for those who endure ties the bond to the holding, not to the result. So the worth of that endurance does not depend on how the day went.

crossReferences.why: Gives their words immediately: a prayer for forgiveness, firm footing and help.
Describes a small band saying many a small group has overcome a large one by God's leave.
Closes the surah with the same vocabulary of endurance and of holding a position.

studies.applyIt: The three verbs here describe a sequence: losing heart, weakening, then giving in. They are not the same thing, and the first can happen without the others following it. Notice which stage you are actually at with something difficult. Most people declare the third when they are only at the first.
studies.explainEasier: Many prophets before this one fought with large groups of devoted people beside them. When hard things hit them, they did not lose heart, they did not grow weak, and they did not give up. God loves people who hold on like that.

studies.title: Their Only Words
studies.meaning: What those earlier companies said under pressure is reported, and the wording insists that it was all they said. The prayer has four parts, and the order is a surprise. It starts with forgiveness, not for wrongs done to others but for their own excess in their affairs. Then it asks for firm feet. Then for help. The early scholars note the order: the request about their own conduct comes first, and the request for victory comes last. Most people under threat would say it the other way round.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the description of earlier communities that met hardship without breaking. The passage sits in the surah's account of Uhud. The classical sources report two things from that day: a dispute over the command, and a rush to collect spoils. The early scholars read the prayer's mention of excess in one's own affairs straight against that background.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to exceed proper measure, used of spending and of any excess. It names overstepping rather than sin in general, so the confession is specific about the kind of failure.
A physical request, using the verb for fixing something in place and the word for feet. In a battle it means not being pushed back, and Arabic uses it for steadiness of resolve as well.
From the root for coming to another's aid, used throughout this surah. Placing it last means the prayer asks for assistance only after it has asked to be repaired and then steadied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A line of men held ground shoulder to shoulder, so the phrase about firm feet was no image to them. Sandals in loose ground, a slope, a stumble over a body: these decided whether a line held. Asking for steady feet was asking for the most solid thing a fighter could want. And it came before asking to win.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer here is quoted in full, and the words before it say that this was the whole of what they said. The Quran keeps a number of such prayers word for word. Several of them are in this surah, which holds more quoted prayers than most chapters of its length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the four requests is the argument. Asking first about their own excess treats the trouble inside as the one that comes first. Asking for firm feet before asking for help treats endurance as the thing really needed. Victory is asked for last, and briefly. That puts the outcome below the state of the people asking for it.

crossReferences.why: Records a nearly identical prayer for firm feet and for help, before an earlier battle.
Gives another prayer preserved in this surah, asking that hearts not swerve after guidance.
Closes the surah with a longer prayer, which also begins with forgiveness.

studies.applyIt: Look at the order of these four requests and compare it with your own prayers under pressure. Most of us begin with the outcome and never reach our own conduct. Try reversing it once this week: ask first about where you have overstepped, and let the request for help come last.
studies.explainEasier: This is all they said when things got hard. They asked God to forgive their sins and the times they went too far. They asked Him to hold their feet steady. Last of all, they asked Him to help them win.

studies.title: The Best Of Helpers
studies.meaning: Three ayat close one thread and open another. Those earlier communities are said to have been given the reward of this world and the better reward of the next, with a closing note about God's love for those who do good. Then a warning to the believers, using the same image of turning on the heels that appeared a few ayat earlier. Then one short sentence that answers it: God is your protector, and He is the best of helpers.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the battle at Uhud, when advice about the community's position and its prospects was coming in from every quarter. The early scholars tie the warning to that pressure. The short ayah after it is read as the surah's answer, given without argument. Its words for protection come back again and again in this section.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to come back, used of a garment returning to its owner. Reward in Arabic is described as something coming back rather than as a payment made from outside.
From the same root as the word for a guardian used earlier in this surah. It covers protector, patron and the one who takes charge of your affairs, all inside a single term.
A superlative built on the root for aid used repeatedly in this surah. The comparative form implies there are other helpers, placing God at the head of a list rather than alone on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: After a defeat, the real question in Arabia was whose protection you would seek next. Beaten groups made new ties fast, because a party with no patron was finished. Advice came at once, and nearly always from someone with a stake in the answer. The warning here belongs to that moment, when a community is weakest and easiest for someone else to move around.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of turning on the heels comes up twice within a few ayat of this surah. Once it is about the death of the Prophet. Here it is about taking bad advice. One image ties two very different dangers together. The Quran uses the phrase in only a handful of places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer to the warning is a statement about a bond, not a plan. Nothing is said about what to do. The community is told whose it is. That meets the real worry of the moment, which was not about tactics but about who would stand behind them. Calling God the best of helpers, rather than the only one, leaves ordinary human help in place underneath.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of turning on the heels, at the news of the Prophet's death.
Names God as protector with the same word, calling Him an excellent protector and helper.
Says shortly afterwards that if God helps you, then no one can overcome you.

studies.applyIt: After a setback, advice arrives quickly and most of it comes from someone with an interest. Think of a recent disappointment and list who offered you a view of it. Then ask, for each of them, what they wanted the situation to become. It is a clarifying exercise, and it takes about two minutes.
studies.explainEasier: God gave those earlier people good things in this life and better ones after it. Then believers are warned: follow people who reject God and you will be turned back and lose. God is your protector, and the best helper there is.

studies.title: Dread Cast Into Hearts
studies.meaning: Something ahead is stated as God's own doing, and it happens inside the other side rather than on the field. Dread will be thrown into their hearts. A reason is given. They set up partners with God for which no warrant was ever sent down. The early scholars note that phrase about warrant. It says their claim has nothing to stand on, not merely that it is wrong. The ayah closes on their lodging, a word for a place you settle into for shelter.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the battle at Uhud. The classical sources report that the attacking force pulled back without pressing its advantage on the city. People at the time found that hard to explain, given the state of the community after that day. The early scholars link this ayah to the withdrawal. The Quran itself states the rule rather than telling the story of any one event.

keyTerms.note: A word for fear that fills and grips, distinguished by the lexicographers from ordinary fear by its suddenness. It names an experience rather than a judgement about how dangerous something is.
From a root meaning power and dominance, used of an argument that compels as well as of a ruler. Here it names the sanction a claim would need in order to stand up at all.
From the verb to take refuge. Using a word for shelter of the fire is a deliberate reversal, since the place sought out for safety is named as the destination instead.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wars in the peninsula were often settled by nerve rather than by losses. A force that lost its confidence pulled back even while it was winning. Commanders knew that spirit could drain away overnight for no reason anyone could see. This was plain experience, not superstition. It made what went on inside an opponent a real thing to reckon with.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for dread appears only a handful of times in the Quran. In every one of them it is put into hearts rather than rising out of a situation. The early scholars note how steady that pattern is across all the places it occurs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What God does here is inward and unseen. That fits the surah's larger argument, that outcomes are not settled by what can be counted. The dread is tied to a cause: a claim made with nothing to back it. So it is not random. What the ayah describes is a state that follows from a false position, not a punishment laid on from outside.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly identical wording of the earlier battle, dread cast into the hearts of opponents.
Describes the same thing again, dread cast in from a direction nobody expected.
States earlier in this surah that help comes only from God, not from visible strength.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this ayah describes something happening inside people, not to them. A position held with nothing behind it is uneasy to hold, whether or not anyone argues with you. If you are defending something you cannot really back up, that unease is telling you something. Name one such position today, even if you keep it.
studies.explainEasier: God says He will put fear into the hearts of the people who fight against the believers. They set up other gods beside Him with nothing to back it up. Their home in the end is the Fire.

studies.title: Until You Faltered
studies.meaning: This is the hardest account of the day. God's promise had been kept, and the other force was being cut down by His leave. Then three things happened in order. You faltered. You argued over the command. You disobeyed, after being shown what you wanted. A split inside the community is then named without softening: some wanted this world, some wanted the next. And the passage ends where nothing in it had prepared for. He pardoned you.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the classical sources agree on the incident behind it. Archers had been placed on high ground with orders to hold their position regardless of how the battle went. When the Meccan force gave way and plunder became visible, most left that position, the ground was retaken, and the day reversed. The Quran's account follows exactly that sequence.

keyTerms.note: A verb whose root covers both sensing and killing, used of harvesting and of striking down. Its use places the community's early success in unmistakably physical terms rather than abstract ones.
From a root meaning to pull in different directions. The form makes it mutual, so what is described is a group tearing at a decision rather than one party overruling another.
From a root meaning to wipe out a trace, used of wind erasing footprints in sand. Pardon in Arabic is the removal of the mark rather than the excusing of the act that made it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Plunder was how a raiding force got paid. Men who rode out expected a share, and taking it carried no shame. For many of them it was the point of the trip. That is what makes the failure at Uhud both ordinary and costly. The archers did what almost any force in Arabia would have done. The position they left was the one thing holding the field.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names three failures in a row: faltering, arguing, and disobeying. Then it splits the community itself into those who wanted this world and those who wanted the next. Few passages in the Quran are as hard on the community they address. And it is kept in that community's own scripture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns down every comfort on offer, then gives one nobody asked for. It does not soften the account. It does not play down the split. It does not blame the enemy's strength. Once the responsibility is fully set out, it ends on pardon, which comes as a gift rather than as a conclusion. Full honesty, then mercy: that is how this surah tends to move.

crossReferences.why: Continues the account, describing the flight and the sorrow that followed it.
Names the cause behind the turning away, and says again that God pardoned them.
Warns against disputing with one another, saying it makes resolve itself depart.

studies.applyIt: The order of this ayah is worth borrowing when you review something that went wrong. Name what actually happened, including your own part in it, in sequence and without adjustment. Then stop. Do not add the excuse or the explanation. The pardon in this passage arrives only once the account is finished.
studies.explainEasier: God kept His promise, and you were beating them. Then you lost your nerve, argued about the orders, and went against them once you saw what you wanted. Some of you wanted this world. Even so, God forgave you.

studies.title: Sorrow Upon Sorrow
studies.meaning: The scene is shown from behind. You were climbing away, not turning back for anyone, while the Messenger called from your rear. Then comes a strange clause. He paid you back with sorrow upon sorrow, so that you would not grieve over what you missed or over what struck you. The early scholars discuss which two sorrows are meant, and they set them out in more than one way. They read the purpose clause this way: a grief given to push out a smaller grief.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the account of Uhud after the position was left. The classical sources describe how confused the retreat was. A rumour went round that the Prophet had been killed, and on that field it was hard to hear anything at all. They report the news that he was alive reaching men who were still scattered. The two sorrows are read against that order of events.

keyTerms.gloss: you were going up and away
keyTerms.note: A verb of ascending and of moving off into open ground. It describes the direction of the retreat physically, up the slope, rather than naming it outright as flight.
From the root for twisting, the same one used earlier in this surah of twisting the tongue. Here it means turning the head, so the denial describes running without a backward glance.
A word for grief that covers and constricts, from a root used of clouds covering over the sky. It names sorrow as something that presses down rather than as sadness merely felt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A retreat up broken ground was chaos. Dust, noise and the slope made it impossible to see or hear more than a few paces, and men lost track of brothers and fathers within moments. Calls from behind were routinely inaudible. The detail that the Messenger was calling from the rear would have been heard as a fact about the field before it was heard as a reproach.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase read as sorrow upon sorrow is one word repeated with a small word between. Arabic uses that shape for layering, not for force. The early scholars disagree about which grief was which. That opening comes from the shape of the phrase itself, not from any gap in the reports.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A second grief is given so that a first will not be felt. That is an odd way to describe mercy. The larger sorrow was the fear that the Prophet had been killed, and it made the smaller ones stop counting: the lost plunder, the wounds. So a greater loss is treated as something that can reorder the small ones, not just add to them. The ayah presents that as meant.

crossReferences.why: Gives the sequence of failures that led to the flight described here.
Continues immediately with the security that came down over part of the force afterwards.
Describes another day when numbers failed and tranquillity was sent down afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Sometimes a large worry arrives and every small one goes quiet. Most people notice that and find it strange. This ayah presents it as intended. Think of a time it happened to you, and notice what the large thing revealed about the size of what it displaced. Keep that ranking when the small ones return.
studies.explainEasier: You ran up the hill and did not look back. The Messenger was calling you from behind. Then God gave you grief on top of grief. That way you would stop aching over what you lost that day.

studies.title: Sleep Sent Down As Security
studies.meaning: After the grief, something is sent down and it is described in two words: security, and then slumber. Sleep on a battlefield is the sign that fear has lifted. But it covers only part of the force. The rest are described as preoccupied with themselves, thinking of God in a way the ayah names as belonging to an earlier age, and asking whether any of the matter was theirs. The answer is given twice, and the passage closes on what hearts are being tested for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the aftermath of the battle at Uhud. The classical sources preserve reports from those present describing a drowsiness that came over them as they sat among the wounded, so heavy that weapons slipped from their hands. The same reports describe others awake through the night, running the day's decisions over. The ayah is read against both accounts.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith and for safety. It names the state rather than the sleep, so the slumber that follows is described as its symptom rather than its cause.
The specific word for the sleep that comes over a person before proper sleep. It names something that arrives rather than something taken, which is why the ayah can describe it as sent down.
A noun formed from the word for ignorance, used of the period before the message came. It names a way of thinking rather than a date, which is why a thought can be described by it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sleep after a battle was the surest measure of a man's state. Some slept where they sat, among the dead, before the field had even been cleared; others walked the camp until dawn. Everyone who had fought knew both conditions and knew which one they had been in. It was not a private matter, since men lay in the open beside each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The same detail, sleep coming over a force around a battle, shows up in the Quran's account of the earlier day at Badr. It is called a security from God there, in almost the same words. Very few bodily experiences are reported twice in the Quran as a sign.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sorts the community by what happened inside them, not by what they did, and it names nobody. The purpose is given at the end: to test what is in the chests and to refine what is in the hearts. A hard day is treated as something that shows what is inward. The sleep of one group becomes a sign only the sleeper can read.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same drowsiness sent down as a security from God, on the earlier day at Badr.
Follows immediately, naming what happened to those who turned back, and the pardon given.
Describes tranquillity sent down into the hearts of believers so that faith would increase.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you do with a night after something has gone badly. Some people sleep and some replay it until morning, and neither is a verdict on anyone's character. But it is information about where you are. Observe yours the next time without judging it, and see what this description sounds like from inside.
studies.explainEasier: After the battle God calmed the believers, and some of them fell asleep right there. Others could only think about themselves and had wrong thoughts about God. God was testing what was really inside them.

studies.title: Some Of What They Earned
studies.meaning: The people who turned back that day are described in one careful sentence. The adversary made them slip, and the reason given is some of what they had earned. That points to an earlier cause without listing it. Then, with nothing in between, the pardon: God has forgiven them. The early scholars note the two names at the close, one about forgiving and one about being slow to anger. They read the second as the unhurried quality that made the pardon possible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the battle at Uhud. The classical sources report that those who had given way heard this ayah with relief. They were named in it and pardoned in the same breath. The early scholars note that it points to no one by name, and does not say what had been earned earlier. So the description stays general while the comfort stays exact.

keyTerms.note: From the root for slipping on smooth ground. The form implies drawing someone into a slip rather than pushing them, so the fault is shared between the one who slipped and what caused it.
A partitive word, so what is named is only part of what they had earned. The commentators note the restraint of the phrasing, which declines both to specify and to exaggerate.
From a root meaning to be slow to anger and deliberate in judgement. It describes patience in one who has power to act at once, which is why it pairs so naturally with forgiveness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Running from a battle was the most public failure open to a man in that world. It was remembered, put into poetry, and used against his family for years. There was no way to set it right. That is why an announced pardon was so unusual. It settled in public what would otherwise have followed those men for life.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the second time in a few ayat that the surah says God pardoned the community after the battle. A different word is used each time. One means to wipe away a trace. The other means to cover over. Together they name both the removal of the mark and the covering of the fault.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does something unusual with blame. In one sentence it names an outside cause, an earlier fault, and a pardon, and none of the three cancels the others. That turns down the choice between blaming a person fully and excusing them fully. The closing name matters too. It describes God as slow and unhurried, and that is what lets an account be settled kindly rather than quickly.

crossReferences.why: Uses a different word for pardon a few ayat earlier, after listing the failures of that day.
Describes the first slip in the same vocabulary, the adversary causing a slipping from a state.
Ends on a similar pairing of pardon and forgiveness, of those with a genuine excuse.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between an excuse and an account. This ayah gives an account: something pushed, something earlier had weakened the footing, and the whole thing is pardoned. Try describing a failure of yours that way once this week, to yourself, in three parts. Notice that the pardon does not require the first two to be untrue.
studies.explainEasier: Some of you ran away on the day the two armies met. Satan made them slip, because of things they had done before. But God has forgiven them. He forgives, and He is never in a hurry.

studies.title: Had They Stayed With Us
studies.meaning: A sentence people say after a death is quoted and then examined. If they had stayed with us, they would not have died. The ayah does not argue with the logic. It names what the sentence does to the person saying it, making it a wearing regret lodged in their own heart, and then states the fact that undoes it: God gives life and gives death. The early scholars note that the instruction is not to stop grieving but to stop building the version in which the loss did not happen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the battle at Uhud. The community lost many men, and some of their families had been against them going. The early scholars tie the quoted sentence to what was being said in the city afterwards, above all by those who had argued against the march. The Quran gives the saying to a group without naming anyone. It speaks to the believers about the habit, not about the speakers.

keyTerms.gloss: they struck out in the land
keyTerms.note: An idiom for travelling, built on the verb to strike. Arabic pictures a journey as striking the ground with the feet, which makes travel an action taken rather than a passage undergone.
From a root meaning to strip bare and to wear out, used of a camel driven past its strength. It names grief that has consumed the person carrying it rather than sorrow simply felt.
Two verbs in a single clause, both with God as their subject. Setting them together removes the space in which a different arrangement of events could have produced a different outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel and raiding were the two ways a young man could lift his family's position. Both carried a real chance of not coming back. Every household had weighed it. Relatives who had urged staying home were sometimes proved right in the most painful way. The sentence quoted in this ayah was heard in the streets of Medina for months.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for regret turns up elsewhere in the Quran. There it names a day of wearing regret at the end of all things. Here it is used of something felt now, about a choice already made and past changing. That puts an ordinary grief in the same class as a final one, as the early scholars note.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The harm of the if-only sentence is placed inside the person who holds it. Nothing is said about whether the reasoning holds up. The objection is practical, not logical: the sentence keeps a wound open and nothing can close it. Naming God as the one who gives life and death then takes away what it rests on. The other history it needs was never there to have.

crossReferences.why: Quotes a version of the same sentence from within the community after the battle.
Reports it again a few ayat later, and answers by asking them to avert death from themselves.
Says nothing befalls you but is written, so you do not grieve over what escapes you.

studies.applyIt: Everyone has a sentence beginning with if only, usually about the same event. Say yours out loud once and notice how well practised it is. Then notice that saying it has never once changed anything, and that it costs you something each time. This ayah is not asking you to feel less. It is asking you to stop rehearsing.
studies.explainEasier: When people die, do not talk like those who say they would still be alive if they had stayed home. That kind of talk only leaves regret in your heart. God is the one who gives life and takes it.

studies.title: Better Than What They Gather
studies.meaning: Two short ayat make the same move twice, with the two verbs swapped between them. If you are killed or you die, forgiveness and mercy from God are better than what others are piling up. If you die or you are killed, the gathering is to God. The early scholars note the swap. Each verb stands first once, so neither way of dying is treated as the one that counts. And the thing being compared is what people gather, not staying alive.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, spoken to a community that had just buried many of its own after the battle at Uhud. Others were telling them how much better it would have been to stay home. The early scholars read the comparison at the end of the first ayah as an answer to that argument. What is set against forgiveness and mercy is what people gather, not the lives they keep.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for gathering things together, used of wealth. Its subject is left as a vague they, which keeps the comparison general rather than aimed at anyone in particular.
A different verb, used of driving people together into one place as a herd is gathered. The passive form leaves the gatherer unnamed and the movement entirely unavoidable.
A conditional particle carrying an emphatic oath, so the clause is stronger than a plain if. Both ayat open with it, which is what gives the pair their insistent rhythm.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's estate was counted the day he died, and what he had gathered passed to others within the week. Everyone had watched an inheritance divided. They knew how fast a lifetime of saving became someone else's property. So setting forgiveness against what people pile up was not a far-off comparison. It measured against something they had just seen change hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs, dying and being killed, appear in both ayat in opposite order, so each one stands first once. The classical scholars of style treat that kind of swap as a known figure. Here it refuses to rank the two ways of dying against each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a reward from God against a pile of goods, and it does not compare like with like. What is offered is not survival but forgiveness. What it is measured against is not life but what people gather. That reframes the argument the community was hearing. The choice being urged on them was never between dying and living. It was between two things to want.

crossReferences.why: Continues the theme a few ayat later, saying those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord.
Compares the enjoyment of this world with the hereafter, and calls the first very little.
Says the enjoyment of this world is small, and the hereafter better for one who is mindful.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you are actually comparing when you weigh a risk. Usually it is safety against danger. This passage changes one side of that scale, setting what you would receive against what you are piling up. Try the same change once with a decision you have been avoiding, and see whether the balance sits differently.
studies.explainEasier: If you are killed or you die while serving God, what He gives you is better than anything other people are saving up. Either way, you are going back to God in the end.

studies.title: Gentleness That Held Them Together
studies.meaning: The ayah calls the manner of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) a gift, then draws a consequence from it. Harshness would have emptied the space around him. Three instructions follow, and their order is deliberate. Pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and then consult them. So the people who had just cost the community a battle are put back into the decisions, not merely excused. Trust is placed after resolve, not instead of it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line comes straight after the review of Uhud. The defeat followed a decision taken by consultation, against the Prophet's own first inclination to stay in the city. Archers leaving their post turned an advantage into a rout. The instruction to keep consulting them arrives exactly where consultation had appeared to fail. Early scholars treat that placement as the force of the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of dough, of pliable wood, of anything that yields under pressure without breaking. The word describes texture rather than mood, so the gentleness is presented as a quality others could feel.
Roughness in manner and word, the opposite of pliable. It is paired here with a second phrase about hardness of heart, separating a harsh way of speaking from the hardness underneath it.
From a root for extracting honey from a comb. Consultation is pictured as drawing out something valuable that is already there, held inside the people being asked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian tribes were led by consent, not by command. A chief held authority because men chose to follow him. He kept them by hearing their views in assembly and sharing out what came in. He took insult without answering it. A leader who humiliated his followers lost them to another tent by morning. The ayah names that plain political fact, then treats the manner that prevents it as a mercy given from outside.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah moves through several addressees inside one sentence. There is a statement about the Prophet's manner, then three commands given to him, then a closing line about whom God loves. Surah 42 is named after the word for consultation. That exact form occurs only once in the Quran, at 42:38, in a list of the qualities of a believing community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is treated here as revelation's tool, not its ornament. The message would not have held people if the messenger had been abrasive. The ayah says so without embarrassment. It grounds the softness in God's mercy rather than in temperament. It also sets a limit on trust in God by placing it after a decision is made. So reliance is what follows resolve, not a substitute for it.

crossReferences.why: Lists mutual consultation among the marks of a community that answers its Lord.
Describes the same messenger as grieved by their hardship and gentle towards believers.
States plainly that he stands upon a great character, in an early Meccan surah.

studies.applyIt: Before the next decision that affects someone else, ask one person who will have to live with it what they think, and let them finish. You are not required to take the advice. Notice instead what asking does to the room, and to how the decision lands once it is made.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet that being gentle was a gift. If he had been harsh, people would have walked away. So forgive them, pray for them, and ask them what they think.

studies.title: If God Helps You
studies.meaning: Two conditions are set out in the same shape, and only one of them is comfortable. If God helps you, nobody overcomes you. If He leaves you without support, who will help you after Him. The early scholars note that the second half is a question, not a threat. It asks the hearer to look for another helper and find none. The instruction then follows from both halves together, not from the first alone: so let the believers rely on God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the part that follows the battle at Uhud. Both halves of this ayah had been shown in a single afternoon. The early scholars read the placing as deliberate, since the community had known help and then its loss on the same day. The ayah still states the rule without tying it to that occasion. That is how the surah usually handles such lessons.

keyTerms.note: A verb for abandoning someone at the moment they need help, used of a companion who steps back in a fight. It names withdrawal by someone expected to stand, which is stronger than simply failing to assist.
An active participle from the root for prevailing. Negating the whole category rather than any particular opponent is what makes the first half absolute rather than comparative.
A command form from the root meaning to appoint an agent to act on your behalf. Reliance in Arabic is a delegation, so it assumes an arrangement made rather than a feeling held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An agent was a familiar figure in Arabian trade. A merchant who could not travel named someone to buy and sell for him. The deal was plain: the agent acted, and the merchant carried the outcome. The verb this ayah uses for reliance comes straight out of that world. It makes trust an appointment you make, not a mood you hold.
studies.didYouKnow: The call to rely on God comes twice in this surah within a few dozen ayat. One is at the opening of the account of the battle, and this one is at its close. The two of them bracket the whole passage. The wording is the same in both places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah will not give a guarantee. It gives a place to put the matter instead. Both halves are stated, so being left without support is admitted rather than denied. What follows is reliance, not confidence about how things turn out. That says something exact about trust. It is not a forecast that things will go well. It is a decision about where the matter is placed.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical instruction at the start of this surah's account of the same battle.
Says whoever relies on God, He is sufficient for him, and His command reaches its end.
Says nothing befalls us except what God has written, and closes on the same instruction.

studies.applyIt: The ayah gives you both halves, so do the same. Take something you are anxious about and write two sentences: what it looks like if it goes well, and what it looks like if it does not. Then notice that the conclusion the passage draws comes after both, not after the first one only.
studies.explainEasier: If God is helping you, nobody can beat you. If He leaves you on your own, nobody else can step in and help. So believers put the whole thing in God's hands.

studies.title: Nothing Taken In Secret
studies.meaning: The word at the centre means taking something quietly from what a group has entrusted to you. It points above all at spoils before they are divided. The ayah says this is not something a prophet does. Then it makes the result vivid. Whoever takes will carry what he took to the Day of Resurrection and bring it with him. The early scholars report that the ayah answered a suspicion after the battle about a missing item. They keep more than one account of what it was.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the battle at Uhud, where leaving a position had itself been tied to the taking of spoils. The classical sources report a suspicion going round about something missing from the collected goods. They read the ayah as an answer to it. Reports of the item itself differ, so the early scholars treat the occasion as clear in outline and unsure in its details.

keyTerms.note: A precise term for removing something from common property before it is distributed. Arabic has a dedicated word for it, which tells you how familiar the problem was in that society.

keyTerms.gloss: he will bring what he took
keyTerms.note: The verb is to come or arrive, so the image is of a person carrying the item into the gathering. Nothing is said about its weight, and the commentators note that the carrying is the point.
The commercial verb used earlier in this surah for a debt discharged completely. Its reappearance places both the taking and the reckoning in the vocabulary of accounts kept and settled.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spoils were gathered into one place and shared out by an agreed method. The whole system rested on nothing leaving the pile first. A man who took an item early gained something small and put the whole arrangement at risk. Everyone knew that. Everyone also knew how easy it was to do in the confusion after a fight.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic has its own verb for taking from common property before it is shared out. It is not the ordinary word for theft. The Quran uses it only in this surah. That a word exists just for this shows how much a fair division of spoils mattered to holding a fighting force together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a suspicion by stating a rule about prophets, not by denying one charge. That method is worth noting. It makes the defence a matter of what a prophet is, not of one man's word. The picture of carrying the item into the gathering does something too. A hidden act becomes an object you can see. That is how the Quran usually shows a covered thing being uncovered at last.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the division of spoils directly, referring the whole matter to God and the Messenger.
Instructs that trusts be rendered back to those they belong to, and that judgement be just.
Uses the same verb for being paid in full, of every soul on a day beyond any doubt.

studies.applyIt: The specific failure here is taking a little from something held in common: an expense claim, a shared resource, time billed but not worked. It is always small, which is exactly why it is easy. Pick one such thing and put it back this week, quietly. Nobody needs to know, which is rather the point.
studies.explainEasier: A prophet would never take things in secret. Anyone who does will have to carry what he took on the Day when everyone stands up again. Then each person gets exactly what he earned, with nothing taken away.

studies.title: Not The Same At All
studies.meaning: A question is asked that answers itself. Is the one who went after God's approval like the one who came away carrying His anger. Then a very short ayah, easy to pass over. They are degrees with God. The wording is unusual. It does not say they have degrees; it says they are degrees. The early scholars read that as making people one with their rank, rather than having a rank handed to them from outside.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section that follows the battle at Uhud. What people did on that single day had varied a great deal. The early scholars tie the pairing to it, since the passage comes straight after a line about taking from the spoils. The question and the words about degrees are read together. They name differences the day itself had made plain.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the word for contentment, used earlier in this surah among the rewards of the mindful. It names the giver's regard rather than any particular gift given.
The verb means to return bearing something, used of a traveller coming home with a load. Displeasure is described as something carried back rather than as something sent after a person.
The plural of a word for a step on a stair. Saying that people are degrees rather than have them collapses the distinction between a person and their standing entirely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Arabian society came from birth, from wealth and from the name of your line. You could see it in where a man sat and when he spoke. Everyone knew the order in a gathering. An ayah saying that people are their own degrees before God cut across all of that. In that world standing was inherited, not built by anything you did.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording that people are degrees, rather than that they have them, turns up in a similar form elsewhere in the Quran. The early scholars of grammar ask whether a word has been left out. Most read the gap as meant. The shorter form ties the person to the rank more tightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats standing before God as something a person becomes, not something handed out. That is what the odd grammar does. It fits the surah's argument that a hard day showed what people already were. The two paths matter too. One is named by what it goes after. The other is named by what it comes back carrying.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same construction of the believers, saying they are degrees with their Lord.
Names God's approval earlier in this surah, among the things better than what is loved here.
Says for all there are degrees according to what they did, and God is not unaware.

studies.applyIt: The question here is rhetorical, which means it expects you to answer it. Take one thing you did this week and ask honestly which of the two descriptions fits: pursuing approval, or coming away carrying something. Most days contain both. Naming which was which is the whole exercise, and it takes a minute.
studies.explainEasier: A person who goes after what pleases God is not the same as a person who ends up with God angry at him. They are not on the same level. God sees exactly what each one does.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among Themselves
studies.meaning: The favour is named and then unpacked in three verbs. A messenger was raised from among the people themselves, and he recites the signs to them, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom. The phrase about being from among themselves carries weight, since it makes the messenger a neighbour rather than a visitor. The ayah closes by naming what came before, described plainly as evident straying, with nothing softened.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, set inside the account of what followed the battle at Uhud. The early scholars note where it falls. A community that had just failed is reminded of what it was given, not of what it did. The three tasks listed here also appear in Abraham's prayer over the sanctuary in an earlier surah. The scholars read this ayah as the answer to that prayer.

keyTerms.note: A verb for granting a benefit, from a root also connected with cutting off. In its good sense it names an unearned gift, and the Quran uses it of favours nobody could have claimed as a right.
Literally from their souls. The phrase makes the messenger one of them in origin and in kind, not merely present among them, which is what the commentators draw out of it.
From a root covering both purity and increase. It names cleansing and growth as one process, so what is removed and what develops are described by a single verb.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia was local. A man listened to someone whose family he knew, whose lineage he could recite, and whose conduct he had watched over years. An outsider carried no weight whatever he said. Being from among themselves was therefore not a detail of biography; it was the precondition for anyone being heard at all.
